query.original_query: word order typology SOV SVO effect on language model reasoning planning and incremental processing

sub_queries.semantic_query: effect of word order typology SOV SVO on language model reasoning planning and incremental processing, probing attention heads and residual stream for syntactic biases
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate how word order typology—specifically SOV versus SVO structures—influences reasoning and incremental processing in autoregressive language models. Using causal probing and activation patching, we analyze attention heads and residual stream representations across multiple model families. Our analysis reveals that attention heads in intermediate layers exhibit systematic biases toward subject-first or verb-final patterns, correlating with the dominant typology of the training data. We find that residual stream states encode hierarchical syntactic dependencies earlier in SOV languages, reflecting a delayed verb resolution strategy, whereas SVO processing shows earlier integration of verb information. Causal mediation analysis further demonstrates that specific attention heads are causally implicated in planning long-distance dependencies, with their ablation disproportionately affecting reasoning accuracy on typologically congruent sentences. Results show that incremental processing difficulty, measured via surprisal and attention entropy, aligns with typological expectations: SOV models exhibit higher uncertainty before the verb, while SVO models show smoother integration. These findings suggest that syntactic biases are not merely superficial but are embedded in the model’s core reasoning circuits.

sub_queries.semantic_query: word order typology SOV SVO effects on human sentence comprehension incremental parsing and planning, cross-linguistic processing differences
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated the influence of basic word order typology (SOV vs. SVO) on incremental sentence processing, using self-paced reading and eye-tracking during reading in two typologically distinct languages. Participants read transitive sentences with temporary ambiguities in relative clause attachment and object-verb dependencies. We measured reading times and fixation durations at the critical verb and post-verbal region. Results indicate that SOV speakers exhibited a processing advantage for verb-final dependencies, with reduced reading times at the verb when the object was encountered earlier, consistent with incremental argument structure building. In contrast, SVO speakers showed increased processing costs at the verb when the object was delayed, reflecting a greater reliance on early verb information for syntactic prediction. Findings support the hypothesis that cross-linguistic differences in word order systematically shape the timing and nature of syntactic parsing and planning operations. These data are consistent with experience-based models of sentence comprehension, wherein language-specific statistical regularities modulate the incremental integration of syntactic and semantic information during real-time processing.

papers.title: Probing for Incremental Parse States in Autoregressive Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent can the syntactic sensitivity of autoregressive language models be attributed to a learned ability to maintain and update implicit representations of incremental syntactic structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a suite of incremental parse probes for autoregressive language models and demonstrates they can predict model preferences on ambiguous sentence prefixes and causally intervene on model representations to steer behavior, suggesting implicit incremental syntactic inferences underlie next-word predictions.
papers.conclusion: The best-performing probe (MAP) incorporates stack-based linguistic constraints while being agnostic to encoding details, suggesting language models not only rediscover linguistic structure through pretraining but learn to make 'inferences' over this structure in real-time comprehension.
papers.key_findings:
The MLP Action Probe (MAP), which incorporates stack-based representations, performs best in parsing and predicting model behavior.
Probes can be used to predict model preferences on ambiguous sentence prefixes, such as NP/Z ambiguities.
Counterfactual perturbations using the probes (especially MAP) can steer model behavior in the expected direction, though effect sizes are small.
Autoregressive language models maintain implicit representations of incremental syntactic structures that mediate next-word predictions.
The geometric probe (GAP) and no-stack probe (NAP) have limitations compared to MAP in representing incremental parse states.
papers.limitation:
The question of what constitutes a probe remains a potential confound.
Counterfactual effects, while significant for many layers, are small in absolute terms.
The probes rely on a particular oracle (ArcStandard); other oracles (e.g., ArcEager) might be better suited.
papers.abstract: Next-word predictions from autoregressive neural language models show remarkable sensitivity to syntax. This work evaluates the extent to which this behavior arises as a result of a learned ability to maintain implicit representations of incremental syntactic structures. We extend work in syntactic probing to the incremental setting and present several probes for extracting incomplete syntactic structure (operationalized through parse states from a stack-based parser) from autoregressive language models. We find that our probes can be used to predict model preferences on ambiguous sentence prefixes and causally intervene on model representations and steer model behavior. This suggests implicit incremental syntactic inferences underlie next-word predictions in autoregressive neural language models.

papers.title: Neural Language Models as Psycholinguistic Subjects: Representations of Syntactic State
papers.research_question: To what extent do neural network language models reflect incremental representations of syntactic state?
papers.core_contribution: Large LSTMs trained on large datasets can represent syntactic state comparably to an explicitly syntactic model (RNNG), and data size is crucial for learning fine-grained lexical cues to syntactic structure.
papers.conclusion: All models show basic incremental syntactic state representation, but capturing fine-grained lexical cues requires large amounts of data, while coarse-grained structure can be learned with either syntactic supervision or large data.
papers.key_findings:
All tested models show basic evidence of incremental syntactic state representation (e.g., subordinate clause licensing).
Only the large LSTMs (GRNN, JRNN) and the RNNG fully capture the proper behavior of subordinate clauses (no-matrix penalty).
All models show NP/Z garden path effects, but only large LSTMs are sensitive to verb transitivity as a cue.
All models show MV/RR garden path effects, but only large LSTMs and the RNNG are sensitive to verb morphology as a cue.
The representation of syntactic state degrades with increasing intervening material in some models (GRNN and TinyLSTM).
future_direction: Using psycholinguistic methodology as a basis for more systematic tests of the linguistic competence of NLP systems.
papers.abstract: We deploy the methods of controlled psycholinguistic experimentation to shed light on the extent to which the behavior of neural network language models reflects incremental representations of syntactic state. To do so, we examine model behavior on artificial sentences containing a variety of syntactically complex structures. We test four models: two publicly available LSTM sequence models of English (Jozefowicz et al., 2016; Gulordava et al., 2018) trained on large datasets; an RNNG (Dyer et al., 2016) trained on a small, parsed dataset; and an LSTM trained on the same small corpus as the RNNG. We find evidence that the LSTMs trained on large datasets represent syntactic state over large spans of text in a way that is comparable to the RNNG, while the LSTM trained on the small dataset does not or does so only weakly.

papers.title: The Truth is in There: Improving Reasoning in Language Models with Layer-Selective Rank Reduction
papers.research_question: Can selectively removing higher-order components of weight matrices in Transformer models improve performance on reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Selectively removing higher-order components of weight matrices via low-rank approximation (LASER) improves LLM performance on reasoning tasks, especially for less frequent facts, by denoising conflicting responses encoded in higher-order components.
papers.conclusion: LASER is an effective post-hoc intervention that improves reasoning by denoising weight matrices, and its success warrants further study on why higher-order components accumulate noise.
papers.key_findings:
LASER improves accuracy on various NLP benchmarks, with the largest gains on facts less frequent in training data.
Improvements are most pronounced when reducing rank in later MLP layers, while early layer reduction harms performance.
LASER increases model robustness to paraphrases of questions.
Higher-order components often encode noisy or conflicting responses (e.g., generic high-frequency words or incorrect answers of the same semantic type).
Composing LASER interventions across multiple layers yields further performance improvements.
papers.limitation:
LASER slightly increases perplexity on the training data, indicating a trade-off between task performance and language modeling fluency.
The improvements in non-text domains (e.g., reinforcement learning) are smaller and less consistent.
future_direction: Understanding why higher-order components in weight matrices accumulate noisy answers during training.
Investigating the effect of model architecture and other structural choices on the occurrence of this phenomenon.
Explaining why the phenomenon is specifically true for later layers in the MLP.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) have become a fixture in modern machine learning. Correspondingly, significant resources are allocated towards research that aims to further advance this technology, typically resulting in models of increasing size that are trained on increasing amounts of data. This work, however, demonstrates the surprising result that it is often possible to significantly improve the performance of LLMs by selectively removing higher-order components of their weight matrices. This simple intervention, which we call LAyer-SElective Rank reduction (LASER), can be done on a model after training has completed, and requires no additional parameters or data. We show extensive experiments demonstrating the generality of this finding across language models and datasets, and provide in-depth analyses offering insights into both when LASER is effective and the mechanism by which it operates.

papers.title: Studying the Inductive Biases of RNNs with Synthetic Variations of Natural Languages
papers.research_question: How do typological properties such as word order and morphological case marking affect the ability of neural sequence models to acquire the syntax of a language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a methodology for generating synthetic languages by parametrically modifying parsed corpora to study the inductive biases of RNNs, and uses it to show that RNNs have a recency bias, that polypersonal agreement improves performance, and that overt case marking facilitates agreement prediction.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methodology is effective for studying grammatical inductive biases of RNNs, and the findings reveal that RNNs exhibit a recency bias, benefit from multitask agreement prediction, and are aided by case marking.
papers.key_findings:
Performance was higher in subject-verb-object order (SVO) than in subject-object-verb order (SOV), suggesting that RNNs have a recency bias.
Predicting agreement with both subject and object (polypersonal agreement) improves over predicting each separately, suggesting that underlying syntactic knowledge transfers across tasks.
Overt morphological case makes agreement prediction significantly easier, regardless of word order.
papers.limitation:
The reordering manipulation is limited to core elements (subjects, objects, and verbs) and does not consider word order inside other types of phrases.
The synthetic languages are simpler than natural languages because word order is completely fixed or fully flexible, while natural languages often have more complex and varied word order patterns.
future_direction: Exploring whether consistent reordering across phrase categories (head directionality parameter) improves model performance.
Conducting human experiments based on the agreement prediction task to compare human and RNN learning.
papers.abstract: How do typological properties such as word order and morphological case marking affect the ability of neural sequence models to acquire the syntax of a language? Cross-linguistic comparisons of RNNs' syntactic performance (e.g., on subject-verb agreement prediction) are complicated by the fact that any two languages differ in multiple typological properties, as well as by differences in training corpus. We propose a paradigm that addresses these issues: we create synthetic versions of English, which differ from English in one or more typological parameters, and generate corpora for those languages based on a parsed English corpus. We report a series of experiments in which RNNs were trained to predict agreement features for verbs in each of those synthetic languages. Among other findings, (1) performance was higher in subject-verb-object order (as in English) than in subject-object-verb order (as in Japanese), suggesting that RNNs have a recency bias; (2) predicting agreement with both subject and object (polypersonal agreement) improves over predicting each separately, suggesting that underlying syntactic knowledge transfers across the two tasks; and (3) overt morphological case makes agreement prediction significantly easier, regardless of word order.

papers.title: Ungrammatical Influences: Evidence for Dynamical Language Processing
papers.research_question: Do ungrammatical influences exist in human sentence processing? Specifically, are readers temporarily distracted by coherent but grammatically incompatible local structures during parsing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence from a connectionist model and human reading experiments that ungrammatical local structures can influence parsing, supporting a dynamical, self-organizing approach to language processing.
papers.conclusion: Ungrammatical influences exist in human sentence processing, and dynamical, self-organizing models like connectionist networks can account for these effects, pointing towards parallel processing solutions to parsing tractability.
papers.key_findings:
A Simple Recurrent Network model shows higher error (Kullback-Leibler Divergence) on sentences containing irrelevant local coherences (e.g., noun-noun compounds) that are grammatically incompatible with the global structure.
Human reading times are slower for sentences containing such ungrammatical local coherences (Experiment 1), indicating distraction by grammatically ruled-out interpretations.
A stronger slowing effect is found for reduced relative clauses with homophonous verbs compared to non-homophonous verbs (Experiment 2), showing the effect extends beyond lexical compounds.
The results suggest that parsing involves competition among local coherences via dynamical feedback, rather than deductive elimination of parses based on top-down constraints.
The connectionist model's behavior aligns with human data, indicating that dynamical, self-organizing mechanisms may address tractability problems in parsing.
papers.limitation:
The effect in the network simulation was somewhat unstable with longer training on the same materials and sometimes reversed itself.
Experiment 1 results could be explained by lexical automaticity (activation of compound senses in the lexicon) rather than syntactic parsing interference, though Experiment 2 addresses this.
future_direction: Further exploration of dynamical parsing models that use feedback and self-organization to handle incoherent structure representation.
Incorporating the problem of incoherent structure representation into the theory of grammar.
papers.abstract: Ungrammatical Inuences: Evidence for Dynamical Language Processing Whitney Tabor tabor@uconnvm.uconn.edu Bruno Galantucci Bruno.Galantucci@uconn.edu Department of Psychology University of Connecticut Storrs, CT 06269 USA Abstract A distinguishing feature of self-organizing models of cog- nitive structure is that they permit incompatible struc- tures to coexist at least temporarily. Here we report on a connectionist model of natural language process- ing which appears to temporarily construct incoherent structures. We then describe two reading-time studies which reveal people exhibiting the same tendency. In particular, both networks and people show sensitivity to the irrelevant structural interpretations of the under- lined phrases in (1) and (2). (1) We did not think the company would re truck drivers without consulting the union rst. (2) The manager watched the waiter served pea soup by the trainee. This kind of sensitivity is absent in parsing models which treat grammatical constraints as absolute because such models lack a principled method of generating incoher- ent parses. Connectionist networks make the right pre- dictions by using feedback and self-organization. Our results push in the direction of seeking a solution to the tractability problems of parsing by using dynamical mechanisms in a parallel architecture. Introduction Current sentence-processing research tends to focus on ambiguity-related processing in sentences like (1) { (3): (1) The mechanic maintained the truck was working beautifully. (2) The cop arrested by the detective was chagrined. (3) The cook stirred the soup with the tomatoes. Each of these sentences has a structural ambiguity which is resolved on the basis of structural or pragmatic infor- mation when the underlined words arrive. Reading time and eye tracking studies show that when biases favor the wrong interpretation initially, readers tend to slow down and/or make regressions in the disambiguating re- gion, which suggests that they either choose the wrong parse initially or are biased toward it (see Frazier, 1988; Tanenhaus & Trueswell, 1995). Such phenomena accord well with a model of sen- tence processing which assumes people construct phrase- structure parses incrementally based on the input up to the current point in time. On this view, the slow-down in the disambiguating region is due either to extra time Figure 1: The Zollner illusion. spent on revising an incorrect parse, or to extra time spent on revising the weighting assigned to dierent pos- sible parses maintained in parallel. Focusing for a moment on cognitive processes outside of sentence processing, there is a good deal of evidence that people are reliably vulnerable to certain adverse inuences when interpreting complex stimuli. In the Zollner illusion (Held, 1971|Figure 1), lines on a page appear to be nonparallel even though retinal and depth of eld information indicate parallelism. Similarly, in the Stroop eect (Stroop, 1966), a decision is supposed to have been made ahead of time to interpret the stimulus along one particular dimension of contrast (e.g. color), and yet when the stimulus is presented, people are often led astray by irrelevant verbal information. These cases are dierent from the classic sentence pro- cessing examples listed in (1) through (3) in that they show people temporarily failing to rule out an interpre- tation that could be ruled out absolutely, given the in- formation at hand. What would be the analogous cases in sentence processing? Denition of Ungrammatical Inuences There is a class of sentences in which one parse of a word sequence can be completely ruled out on grammatical grounds and yet (we hypothesize) people are inuenced by it anyway. The following are examples of such hy- pothesized \Ungrammatical Inuences : (4) a. They won't re truck drivers on Sunday. b. They won't hire truck drivers on Sunday.

papers.title: Comparison of Structural Parsers and Neural Language Models as Surprisal Estimators
papers.research_question: How do structural parsers and neural language models compare as surprisal estimators for predicting human sentence processing difficulty?
papers.core_contribution: The proposed structural parser, which incorporates strong linguistic generalizations, achieves comparable or superior fits to human reading times compared to neural language models trained on much more data. Among GPT-2 models, smaller models with fewer parameters fit human data better when training data is held constant.
papers.conclusion: Incremental parsers that embody strong linguistic generalizations are more appropriate as computational-level models of human sentence processing than deep neural language models, which require orders of magnitude more training data and do not provide a better fit to human reading behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Surprisal estimates from the structural parser deliver comparable and often superior fits to self-paced reading and eye-tracking data compared to neural language models.
Among GPT-2 models sharing the same architecture and training data, there is a negative correlation between parameter count and fit to self-paced reading and eye-tracking data.
The character-based morphological word model in the structural parser makes a large contribution to regression model fit, suggesting a role for subword information in sentence processing.
Surprisal estimates from the structural parser and 5-gram model did not contribute as much to fMRI data model fit compared to neural LMs, suggesting different measures are sensitive to different aspects of processing difficulty.
The relationship between language model perplexity and psychometric predictive power is influenced by primary architecture and training data amount, not just model capacity.
future_direction: Future work should continue to focus on incorporating relevant linguistic generalizations into concrete models and evaluating their predictions on human subject data.
papers.abstract: Expectation-based theories of sentence processing posit that processing difficulty is determined by predictability in context. While predictability quantified via surprisal has gained empirical support, this representation-agnostic measure leaves open the question of how to best approximate the human comprehender's latent probability model. This article first describes an incremental left-corner parser that incorporates information about common linguistic abstractions such as syntactic categories, predicate-argument structure, and morphological rules as a computational-level model of sentence processing. The article then evaluates a variety of structural parsers and deep neural language models as cognitive models of sentence processing by comparing the predictive power of their surprisal estimates on self-paced reading, eye-tracking, and fMRI data collected during real-time language processing. The results show that surprisal estimates from the proposed left-corner processing model deliver comparable and often superior fits to self-paced reading and eye-tracking data when compared to those from neural language models trained on much more data. This may suggest that the strong linguistic generalizations made by the proposed processing model may help predict humanlike processing costs that manifest in latency-based measures, even when the amount of training data is limited. Additionally, experiments using Transformer-based language models sharing the same primary architecture and training data show a surprising negative correlation between parameter count and fit to self-paced reading and eye-tracking data. These findings suggest that large-scale neural language models are making weaker generalizations based on patterns of lexical items rather than stronger, more humanlike generalizations based on linguistic structure.

papers.title: Syntactic Perturbations Reveal Representational Correlates of Hierarchical Phrase Structure in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: What aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by pretrained language model representations, and how are they built along the layers of the network?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that input perturbations reveal how transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, and that such perturbations are a useful analysis tool for interpreting deep language models.
papers.conclusion: Transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, and attention changes partially explain this sensitivity.
papers.key_findings:
Representations are more distorted by shuffling small n-grams in early layers and by large n-grams in later layers, indicating increasing context scale along layers.
Swapping phrases causes less distortion than swapping non-phrases, indicating sensitivity to phrase structure.
Swapping adjacent words across phrase boundaries causes more distortion than within boundaries, and distortion increases with syntactic distance, especially in deeper layers.
Attention changes partially explain the sensitivity to syntactic distance.
The distortion metric correlates with impairment of syntactic probes (POS, grandparent tags, tree distance).
future_direction: Developing a formal theory of efficient hierarchical data representations in distributed features.
Searching for causal connection between attention structure, representational geometry, and model performance.
Applying perturbation analyses to models trained on shuffled data or models with explicit syntax.
papers.abstract: While vector-based language representations from pretrained language models have set a new standard for many NLP tasks, there is not yet a complete accounting of their inner workings. In particular, it is not entirely clear what aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by these representations, nor how (if at all) they are built along the stacked layers of the network. In this paper, we aim to address such questions with a general class of interventional, input perturbation-based analyses of representations from pretrained language models. Importing from computational and cognitive neuroscience the notion of representational invariance, we perform a series of probes designed to test the sensitivity of these representations to several kinds of structure in sentences. Each probe involves swapping words in a sentence and comparing the representations from perturbed sentences against the original. We experiment with three different perturbations: (1) random permutations of n-grams of varying width, to test the scale at which a representation is sensitive to word position; (2) swapping of two spans which do or do not form a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to global phrase structure; and (3) swapping of two adjacent words which do or do not break apart a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to local phrase structure. Results from these probes collectively suggest that Transformers build sensitivity to larger parts of the sentence along their layers, and that hierarchical phrase structure plays a role in this process. More broadly, our results also indicate that structured input perturbations widens the scope of analyses that can be performed on often-opaque deep learning systems, and can serve as a complement to existing tools (such as supervised linear probes) for interpreting complex black-box models. 1

papers.title: Under the Shadow of Babel: How Language Shapes Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Do different languages lead LLMs to think differently? Do LLMs internalize the cognitive biases embedded in different languages, specifically in causal reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces BICAUSE, a structured bilingual dataset for causal reasoning, and provides empirical evidence that LLMs internalize language-specific reasoning biases, showing typologically aligned attention patterns and a shared understanding when reasoning succeeds.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit language-specific biases in causal reasoning that impact performance, but when reasoning succeeds, they form a shared understanding that transcends surface linguistic form.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit typologically aligned attention patterns, focusing more on causes and sentence-initial connectives in Chinese, while showing a more balanced distribution in English.
Models internalize language-specific preferences for causal word order and often rigidly apply them to atypical inputs, leading to degraded performance, especially in Chinese.
When causal reasoning succeeds, model representations converge toward semantically aligned abstractions across languages, indicating a shared understanding beyond surface form.
Attention patterns over syntactic components show consistent layerwise trends but differ in absolute weights between Chinese and English, reflecting language-specific structural biases.
The similarity of layerwise attention patterns (measured by SVCCA) correlates with reasoning accuracy across different input structures and languages.
papers.limitation:
Focuses exclusively on Chinese and English, representing only a small portion of the world's linguistic diversity.
Does not encompass all model architectures or training paradigms.
Primarily focuses on attention patterns and hidden representations; does not incorporate additional interpretability methods.
future_direction: Extending BICAUSE to a broader set of languages.
Advancing research on multilingual interpretability and alignment mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Language is not only a tool for communication but also a medium for human cognition and reasoning. If, as linguistic relativity suggests, the structure of language shapes cognitive patterns, then large language models (LLMs) trained on human language may also internalize the habitual logical structures embedded in different languages. To examine this hypothesis, we introduce BICAUSE, a structured bilingual dataset for causal reasoning, which includes semantically aligned Chinese and English samples in both forward and reversed causal forms. Our study reveals three key findings: (1) LLMs exhibit typologically aligned attention patterns, focusing more on causes and sentence-initial connectives in Chinese, while showing a more balanced distribution in English. (2) Models internalize language-specific preferences for causal word order and often rigidly apply them to atypical inputs, leading to degraded performance, especially in Chinese. (3) When causal reasoning succeeds, model representations converge toward semantically aligned abstractions across languages, indicating a shared understanding beyond surface form. Overall, these results suggest that LLMs not only mimic surface linguistic forms but also internalize the reasoning biases shaped by language. Rooted in cognitive linguistic theory, this phenomenon is for the first time empirically verified through structural analysis of model internals.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language when processing non-English prompts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that multilingual language models like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate representations favoring English before shifting to the target language.
papers.conclusion: The evidence suggests that the abstract 'concept space' in multilingual transformers lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding linguistic biases.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate embeddings in middle layers decode to English versions of the correct next token, even when the input and output are non-English.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space (high entropy, no language), concept space (low entropy, English dominates), and output space (target language dominates).
The concept space is biased towards English, indicating an internal pivot language.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The token energy metric shows that latent embeddings have low energy in middle layers and high energy in later layers when the target language is selected.
papers.limitation:
Focus on the Llama-2 family limits generalizability to other models.
Tasks are simple and provide a highly controlled, toy-like context.
Limited understanding of the structure of the concept space in its original high-dimensional form.
The logit lens only grants approximate access to internal beliefs about output; other information remains hidden.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias changes when decreasing the dominance of English during training, e.g., by using different language mixtures or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks, including more culturally sensitive problems and popular use-cases.
Better understand and map out the concept space in its high-dimensional form.
papers.abstract: We ask whether multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language -- a question of key importance for understanding how language models function and the origins of linguistic bias. Focusing on the Llama-2 family of transformer models, our study uses carefully constructed non-English prompts with a unique correct single-token continuation. From layer to layer, transformers gradually map an input embedding of the final prompt token to an output embedding from which next-token probabilities are computed. Tracking intermediate embeddings through their high-dimensional space reveals three distinct phases, whereby intermediate embeddings (1) start far away from output token embeddings; (2) already allow for decoding a semantically correct next token in the middle layers, but give higher probability to its version in English than in the input language; (3) finally move into an input-language-specific region of the embedding space. We cast these results into a conceptual model where the three phases operate in "input space", "concept space", and "output space", respectively. Crucially, our evidence suggests that the abstract "concept space" lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding the biases held by multilingual language models.

papers.title: How to Plant Trees in Language Models: Data and Architectural Effects on the Emergence of Syntactic Inductive Biases
papers.research_question: What architectural features and pre-training data properties contribute to the emergence of hierarchical syntactic inductive biases in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that model depth is more critical than width for hierarchical syntactic generalization in Transformers, and that pre-training on simpler language like child-directed speech induces such biases with orders-of-magnitude less data than web text.
papers.conclusion: The study finds that model depth is more important than other architectural components for hierarchical generalization, and that simpler pre-training data leads to faster acquisition of syntactic inductive biases, suggesting Transformers may be more data-efficient in cognitively plausible settings.
papers.key_findings:
Model depth has a greater impact on hierarchical generalization than model width or number of parameters alone.
Pre-training on child-directed speech enables hierarchical generalization with far less data (5M words) compared to Wikipedia or web text (100M-1B words).
The number of parameters does not monotonically predict syntactic generalization accuracy.
Syntactic generalization accuracy correlates with language modeling performance and downstream task performance.
Simpler language, such as Simple Wikipedia, also induces hierarchical biases more efficiently than standard Wikipedia.
papers.limitation:
Findings may not generalize to other types of encoder-decoder models, encoder-only, or decoder-only models.
Analysis is based only on English and two syntactic transformations, which may not cover all linguistic phenomena.
future_direction: Using methods to measure the tree-likeness of Transformer representations during pre-training.
Disentangling the effects of lexical and syntactic complexity in pre-training data.
Exploring a two-phase 'starting small' pre-training approach.
papers.abstract: Accurate syntactic representations are essential for robust generalization in natural language. Recent work has found that pre-training can teach language models to rely on hierarchical syntactic features - as opposed to incorrect linear features - when performing tasks after fine-tuning. We test what aspects of pre-training are important for endowing encoder-decoder Transformers with an inductive bias that favors hierarchical syntactic generalizations. We focus on architectural features (depth, width, and number of parameters), as well as the genre and size of the pre-training corpus, diagnosing inductive biases using two syntactic transformation tasks: question formation and passivization, both in English. We find that the number of parameters alone does not explain hierarchical generalization: model depth plays greater role than model width. We also find that pre-training on simpler language, such as child-directed speech, induces a hierarchical bias using an order-of-magnitude less data than pre-training on more typical datasets based on web text or Wikipedia; this suggests that in cognitively plausible language acquisition settings, neural language models may be more data-efficient than previously thought.

papers.title: Word Order Does Matter (And Shuffled Language Models Know It)
papers.research_question: Do shuffled language models still have traces of word order information? Why is there a gap in performance between models without position embeddings and models trained on shuffled tokens? Are there NLU benchmarks, other than GLUE, on which shuffled language models perform poorly?
papers.core_contribution: Shuffled language models retain word order information due to cues like adjacent BPE symbols and sentence length correlations, and word order is important for some NLU tasks beyond GLUE.
papers.conclusion: Shuffled language models retain word order knowledge largely at the local level due to cues like adjacent BPE symbols and sentence length correlations, and the order of shuffling (before or after BPE) influences this acquisition. Some NLU tasks are sensitive to word order.
papers.key_findings:
Shuffled language models contain substantial information about naturalistic word order, as shown by probing tasks.
The performance gap between models without position embeddings and shuffled models is due to position embeddings providing inductive bias and the presence of local n-grams when shuffling before BPE segmentation.
Even when shuffling after segmentation, models retain some word order information due to statistical dependencies between sentence length and unigram probabilities.
Attention patterns in shuffled models show a preference for adjacent tokens, mimicking convolutional windows.
Some NLU tasks (e.g., Winograd Schema, BoolQ, ReCoRD) are more sensitive to word order and show larger performance drops for shuffled models.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that language models pretrained and/or fine-tuned on randomly permuted sentences exhibit competitive performance on GLUE, putting into question the importance of word order information. Somewhat counter-intuitively, some of these studies also report that position embeddings appear to be crucial for models' good performance with shuffled text. We probe these language models for word order information and investigate what position embeddings learned from shuffled text encode, showing that these models retain information pertaining to the original, naturalistic word order. We show this is in part due to a subtlety in how shuffling is implemented in previous work -- before rather than after subword segmentation. Surprisingly, we find even Language models trained on text shuffled after subword segmentation retain some semblance of information about word order because of the statistical dependencies between sentence length and unigram probabilities. Finally, we show that beyond GLUE, a variety of language understanding tasks do require word order information, often to an extent that cannot be learned through fine-tuning.

papers.title: Examining the Inductive Bias of Neural Language Models with Artificial\n Languages
papers.research_question: What are the inductive biases of neural language models with respect to typological features such as word order, and do these biases reflect tendencies in attested natural languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel method using artificial languages to investigate inductive biases of language models in a controlled causal framework, and finds that transformers and LSTMs exhibit different inductive biases regarding word order, with transformers showing clear preferences and LSTMs showing little preference.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a novel methodology using carefully controlled artificial languages to study inductive biases, finding that LSTMs and transformers have starkly different inductive biases with respect to word order, with LSTMs showing little variation and transformers showing significant variation across languages.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM-based language models show little preference for any particular word ordering across the artificial languages.
Transformer-based language models show clear preferences for some word orderings over others.
The inductive biases of neither LSTM nor transformer architectures reflect tendencies observed in attested natural languages (e.g., transformers perform similarly on common SOV and rare OVS orders).
The proposed method of using artificial languages allows for controlled causal claims about the effect of typological features on model performance.
Mixed-effects modeling reveals specific interaction effects between typological switches for transformers, but not for LSTMs.
papers.limitation: The artificial grammars are simple and do not cover all possible constructions found in natural languages.
future_direction: Extending the base grammars to test additional hypotheses.
Exploring automated methods for assigning weights to grammar productions.
papers.abstract:
Since language models are used to model a wide variety of languages, it is
natural to ask whether the neural architectures used for the task have
inductive biases towards modeling particular types of languages. Investigation
of these biases has proved complicated due to the many variables that appear in
the experimental setup. Languages vary in many typological dimensions, and it
is difficult to single out one or two to investigate without the others acting
as confounders. We propose a novel method for investigating the inductive
biases of language models using artificial languages. These languages are
constructed to allow us to create parallel corpora across languages that differ
only in the typological feature being investigated, such as word order. We then
use them to train and test language models. This constitutes a fully controlled
causal framework, and demonstrates how grammar engineering can serve as a
useful tool for analyzing neural models. Using this method, we find that
commonly used neural architectures exhibit different inductive biases: LSTMs
display little preference with respect to word ordering, while transformers
display a clear preference for some orderings over others. Further, we find
that neither the inductive bias of the LSTM nor that of the transformer appears
to reflect any tendencies that we see in attested natural languages.

papers.title: Does Syntax Need to Grow on Trees? Sources of Hierarchical Inductive Bias in Sequence-to-Sequence Networks
papers.research_question: Which architectural factors affect the generalization behavior of neural sequence-to-sequence models trained on syntactic tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The only architectural factor that consistently imparted a hierarchical bias across syntactic tasks was the use of a tree-structured model with explicit parse tree input, suggesting human-like syntactic generalization requires architectural syntactic structure.
papers.conclusion: Many architectural factors can affect inductive biases, but human-like syntactic generalization may require explicit tree structure in the model when learning from text alone.
papers.key_findings:
The type of recurrent unit (SRN, GRU, LSTM) and attention mechanism (none, location-based, content-based) qualitatively affect inductive biases, but do not consistently lead to hierarchical generalization.
LSTMs and GRUs exhibit different inductive biases, partly due to squashing in GRUs.
Only tree-based models given correct parse trees consistently showed hierarchical generalization across both question formation and tense reinflection tasks.
Sequential models failed to generalize hierarchically even when provided with bracketed input or trained in a multi-task setting.
Tree-based models are not constrained to hierarchical generalizations; they can learn linear transformations if trained on unambiguous data.
papers.limitation:
Humans may have a stronger bias to share processing across phenomena than neural networks, so multi-task learning might be more effective for humans.
Children's input might contain utterances unambiguously supporting hierarchical transformations, whereas the training data assumed a complete lack of such examples.
The training data omits many cues to hierarchical structure available to children, such as prosody and real-world grounding.
The hierarchical bias in tree-based models only emerged when provided with correct parse trees; it is unclear how to effectively use tree-based models without correct parses.
future_direction: Characterization of the effects of hyperparameters and random seeds on generalization.
Investigation of how to effectively use tree-based models without providing correct parses.
Exploration of additional secondary tasks in multi-task learning to impart hierarchical biases.
papers.abstract: Learners that are exposed to the same training data might generalize differently due to differing inductive biases. In neural network models, inductive biases could in theory arise from any aspect of the model architecture. We investigate which architectural factors affect the generalization behavior of neural sequence-to-sequence models trained on two syntactic tasks, English question formation and English tense reinflection. For both tasks, the training set is consistent with a generalization based on hierarchical structure and a generalization based on linear order. All architectural factors that we investigated qualitatively affected how models generalized, including factors with no clear connection to hierarchical structure. For example, LSTMs and GRUs displayed qualitatively different inductive biases. However, the only factor that consistently contributed a hierarchical bias across tasks was the use of a tree-structured model rather than a model with sequential recurrence, suggesting that human-like syntactic generalization requires architectural syntactic structure.

papers.title: Using Priming to Uncover the Organization of Syntactic Representations in Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How are syntactic representations organized in neural language models? Specifically, do LSTM language models track abstract syntactic properties such as the presence of a gap in relative clauses?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a novel technique based on syntactic priming to analyze the organization of syntactic representations in neural language models. It finds that LSTM LMs' representations of sentences with relative clauses are organized hierarchically and track abstract properties like the presence of a gap.
papers.conclusion: The proposed priming technique reveals that LSTM language models organize syntactic representations in a linguistically interpretable manner, tracking abstract properties, though this ability diminishes with more training data.
papers.key_findings:
Sentences with the same syntactic structure are more similar to each other in the LM's representation space than lexically matched sentences with different structures.
Sentences with different types of relative clauses are more similar to each other than to sentences without relative clauses, suggesting LMs track the abstract property of having a gap.
LMs track linguistically interpretable features like reduction and passivity in relative clauses, with passivity contributing more to similarity than reduction.
For some linguistically interpretable classes, similarity between sentences is driven by more than just shared function words, indicating LMs track abstract properties.
The ability to track abstract properties decreases as the training corpus size increases.
papers.limitation:
For classes of sentences that do not share any function words (e.g., all relative clauses), the similarity between sentences in the LM's representation space may be driven purely by lexical items rather than abstract properties.
The hypothesis that similarity between object RCs and other RCs would predict agreement prediction accuracy was not supported.
future_direction: Explore how to bias models to track linguistically useful properties through architectural biases, training on auxiliary tasks, or data augmentation.
Generate a similarity matrix for human representations using priming experiments and compare with LM representations to gain insight into how human-like the LM representations are.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) perform well on tasks that require sensitivity to syntactic structure. Drawing on the syntactic priming paradigm from psycholinguistics, we propose a novel technique to analyze the representations that enable such success. By establishing a gradient similarity metric between structures, this technique allows us to reconstruct the organization of the LMs' syntactic representational space. We use this technique to demonstrate that LSTM LMs' representations of different types of sentences with relative clauses are organized hierarchically in a linguistically interpretable manner, suggesting that the LMs track abstract properties of the sentence.

papers.title: Emergent effects of scaling on the functional hierarchies within large language models
papers.research_question: What is the functional hierarchy of abstraction across layers in LLMs, and how does it change with model scaling?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models exhibit functional hierarchies with abstraction increasing across layers, but scaling introduces deviations such as double representation peaks and anti-persistent fluctuations in attention mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms functional hierarchies in LLMs but reveals emergent deviations with scaling, such as double representation peaks and layer coordination, complicating interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Item-level semantics are most strongly represented in early layers (2-7), two-item relations in middle layers (8-12), and four-item analogies in later layers (10-15), consistent with an abstraction hierarchy.
Deep layers can represent narrow two-item relations from early in the context, suggesting information compression without meaningful abstraction.
In the large Llama-3.3-70b-Instruct model, representation of two-item relations and analogies shows two distinct peaks (layers 12-16 and 25-33), indicating fluctuations in abstraction level.
Adjacent layers in the large model exhibit anti-persistent fluctuations in attention outputs, with negative autocorrelation, suggesting coordinated specialization.
Buried concepts (target text followed by filler) are represented in deeper layers, showing that late layers capture global document-wide information.
papers.limitation:
The interpretation of the double-peak pattern and valley in large models is unclear and requires further work.
Analyses on grammar and syntax were inconclusive and not reported, limiting insights into syntactic processing.
future_direction: Study larger models to understand scaling effects further.
Investigate the mechanisms behind the double-peak representation and layer coordination.
Explore how late-layer representations can be used for steering and safety applications.
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) architectures are often described as functionally hierarchical: Early layers process syntax, middle layers begin to parse semantics, and late layers integrate information. The present work revisits these ideas. This research submits simple texts to an LLM (e.g., "A church and organ") and extracts the resulting activations. Then, for each layer, support vector machines and ridge regressions are fit to predict a text's label and thus examine whether a given layer encodes some information. Analyses using a small model (Llama-3.2-3b; 28 layers) partly bolster the common hierarchical perspective: Item-level semantics are most strongly represented early (layers 2-7), then two-item relations (layers 8-12), and then four-item analogies (layers 10-15). Afterward, the representation of items and simple relations gradually decreases in deeper layers that focus on more global information. However, several findings run counter to a steady hierarchy view: First, although deep layers can represent document-wide abstractions, deep layers also compress information from early portions of the context window without meaningful abstraction. Second, when examining a larger model (Llama-3.3-70b-Instruct), stark fluctuations in abstraction level appear: As depth increases, two-item relations and four-item analogies initially increase in their representation, then markedly decrease, and afterward increase again momentarily. This peculiar pattern consistently emerges across several experiments. Third, another emergent effect of scaling is coordination between the attention mechanisms of adjacent layers. Across multiple experiments using the larger model, adjacent layers fluctuate between what information they each specialize in representing. In sum, an abstraction hierarchy often manifests across layers, but large models also deviate from this structure in curious ways.

papers.title: Diverging views on the role of structured representations in linguistics and language modeling
papers.research_question: How do language models compare to human language processing in terms of structured representations, and what is their role in the science of language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that language models struggle with structured representations central to human language, and suggests that for language models to be effective models of language, structured representations must be incorporated as computational objects.
papers.conclusion: Language models need to conceptualize structured representations as computational objects to better align with human language and contribute to the science of language.
papers.key_findings:
Language models trained on next-word prediction may not learn structure-dependent representations necessary for human language.
Models like ChatGPT show insensitivity to Binding Principle C, incorrectly allowing co-reference in prohibited contexts.
Language models do not make a qualitative distinction between possible and impossible languages, treating them similarly unlike humans.
The internal representational infrastructure for possible and impossible languages overlaps in models, indicating no fundamental difference.
Incorporating structured representations as primary computational targets could enhance language models' utility as models of language.
future_direction: Incorporate structured representations as computational objects in language modeling.
papers.abstract: Recent years have seen dramatic advances in the linguistic abilities of language models, leading some authors to argue that they can be treated as models of language. Against this background, we provide a cognitive perspective on the place of language models in the science of language, with a particular focus on the role of structured representations. Evidence from linguistics, psychology and cognitive neuroscience shows that structured representations occupy a central place in the human mind. Structured representations constrain how linguistic forms map onto meanings, thereby determining the boundaries of possible human languages. In language modeling, instead, the place of structured representations is often peripheral. They are seen as optional end point of modeling, to be induced as a consequence of the objective the model tries to optimize – that is, next-word prediction. Because structured relations and representations are not necessarily useful for predicting the next word in a sequence, it is not guaranteed that the model’s internal organization will come to encode those representations. Indeed, contemporary language models struggle to use structured representations functionally to map form onto meaning, and to determine whether they should consider their input as a possible human language or not. Building on classic insights in linguistics and (computational) cognitive science, we suggest that any use of language models as models of language requires conceptualizing the role of structured representations as computational objects.

papers.title: When Does Syntax Mediate Neural Language Model Performance? Evidence from Dropout Probes
papers.research_question: When do language models use syntactic information causally? How can we design probes to avoid false negatives due to redundant encodings of syntax?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces dropout probes, a new neural probing architecture that encourages probes to use all relevant representations of syntax in model embeddings, enabling better causal analysis and performance improvement via syntactic information injection.
papers.conclusion: Dropout probes are effective for causal analysis of language models and can be used to improve model performance by injecting syntactic information, but further work is needed to extend the approach.
papers.key_findings:
Models encode syntactic information redundantly in their embeddings.
Dropout probes reveal causal use of syntactic representations in QA models where prior methods did not.
Injecting syntactic information at test time can improve QA model performance on syntactically challenging tasks.
NLI models do not show causal use of syntax even with dropout probes.
Dropout probes can boost model performance without retraining.
papers.limitation:
Systematic evaluation of models for many layers, multiple probes, and many counterfactuals is computationally challenging.
The transparency benefits require access to the internals of the pretrained model.
The technique is limited to diagnosis of existing models and does not train models to respond appropriately to interventions.
future_direction: Studying pretrained models beyond those considered in this work.
Further research into redundancy in embeddings.
More investigation into inserting symbolic knowledge into neural representations.
New methods for training models to respond appropriately to interventions.
papers.abstract: Recent causal probing literature reveals when language models and syntactic probes use similar representations. Such techniques may yield "false negative" causality results: models may use representations of syntax, but probes may have learned to use redundant encodings of the same syntactic information. We demonstrate that models do encode syntactic information redundantly and introduce a new probe design that guides probes to consider all syntactic information present in embeddings. Using these probes, we find evidence for the use of syntax in models where prior methods did not, allowing us to boost model performance by injecting syntactic information into representations.

papers.title: Why think step by step? Reasoning emerges from the locality of experience
papers.research_question: Why is chain-of-thought reasoning useful in language models? The paper tests the hypothesis that reasoning is effective when training data consists of overlapping local clusters of variables that influence each other strongly.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that chain-of-thought reasoning is effective when training data has local structure, allowing models to chain accurate local inferences to estimate relationships between variables not seen together in training.
papers.conclusion: The effectiveness of chain-of-thought reasoning in language models is rooted in the local statistical structure of the training data.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning through intermediate variables reduces bias in conditional probability estimation when training data is locally structured.
Free generation, where the model chooses intermediate variables, performs similarly to scaffolded generation with ideal intermediates.
Reasoning does not help when training data is fully observed or has the wrong locality structure.
The combination of locally structured training data and reasoning is more data-efficient than training on fully observed data.
When models fail to estimate conditional probabilities accurately, their estimates tend to match marginal probabilities.
papers.limitation: The study uses a simplified synthetic setting, which may not fully capture natural language data.
papers.abstract: Humans have a powerful and mysterious capacity to reason. Working through a set of mental steps enables us to make inferences we would not be capable of making directly even though we get no additional data from the world. Similarly, when large language models generate intermediate steps (a chain of thought) before answering a question, they often produce better answers than they would directly. We investigate why and how chain-of-thought reasoning is useful in language models, testing the hypothesis that reasoning is effective when training data consists of overlapping local clusters of variables that influence each other strongly. These training conditions enable the chaining of accurate local inferences to estimate relationships between variables that were not seen together in training. We prove that there will exist a "reasoning gap", where reasoning through intermediate variables reduces bias, for the simple case of an autoregressive density estimator trained on local samples from a chain-structured probabilistic model. We then test our hypothesis experimentally in more complex models, training an autoregressive language model on samples from Bayes nets but only including a subset of variables in each sample. We test language models' ability to match conditional probabilities with and without intermediate reasoning steps, finding that intermediate steps are only helpful when the training data is locally structured with respect to dependencies between variables. The combination of locally structured observations and reasoning is much more data-efficient than training on all variables. Our results illustrate how the effectiveness of reasoning step by step is rooted in the local statistical structure of the training data.

papers.title: Disjoint Processing Mechanisms of Hierarchical and Linear Grammars in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) demonstrate distinct, localizable mechanisms for processing hierarchically structured vs. linearly structured sentences that are otherwise superficially identical?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs develop distinct, localizable components for processing hierarchical grammatical structures that are separate from those processing linear structures, and this functional specialization emerges from exposure to language data without human-like inductive biases.
papers.conclusion: Functional specialization toward hierarchical linguistic structure can arise in LLMs solely from exposure to large-scale language distributions, even in the absence of strong human-like inductive biases.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are more accurate at grammaticality judgments for hierarchical inputs than for linear inputs.
The model components (neurons) causally responsible for processing hierarchical grammars show high overlap with each other but low overlap with those responsible for linear grammars.
Ablating hierarchy-sensitive components significantly reduces accuracy on hierarchical grammars but has a lesser effect on linear grammars, and vice-versa.
Hierarchy-sensitive components identified using natural language are also active and influential when processing grammars constructed from nonce words (Jabberwocky sentences), indicating sensitivity to abstract structure rather than meaning or in-distribution language.
papers.limitation: LLMs are trained on data containing multiple languages, unlike the human subjects in the original study who were fluent only in their native language and tested on unfamiliar ones.
future_direction: Investigating cross-linguistic generalization of hierarchical processing mechanisms.
Exploring the role of scale (model size and dataset size) in the emergence of functional specialization.
papers.abstract: All natural languages are structured hierarchically. In humans, this structural restriction is neurologically coded: when two grammars are presented with identical vocabularies, brain areas responsible for language processing are only sensitive to hierarchical grammars. Using large language models (LLMs), we investigate whether such functionally distinct hierarchical processing regions can arise solely from exposure to large-scale language distributions. We generate inputs using English, Italian, Japanese, or nonce words, varying the underlying grammars to conform to either hierarchical or linear/positional rules. Using these grammars, we first observe that language models show distinct behaviors on hierarchical versus linearly structured inputs. Then, we find that the components responsible for processing hierarchical grammars are distinct from those that process linear grammars; we causally verify this in ablation experiments. Finally, we observe that hierarchy-selective components are also active on nonce grammars; this suggests that hierarchy sensitivity is not tied to meaning, nor in-distribution inputs.

papers.title: Structural Persistence in Language Models: Priming as a Window into Abstract Language Representations
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether modern neural language models exhibit structural priming, what factors influence the priming effect, and the nature of the structural representations they acquire.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer language models exhibit structural priming, indicating they encode abstract structural information, and that this priming is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, with evidence for hierarchical syntactic representations.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that Transformer language models are susceptible to structural priming, revealing they encode abstract structural information that is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, and may involve hierarchical syntax.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer language models show evidence of structural priming.
Priming strength is boosted by semantic similarity and lexical overlap between prime and target sentences.
Priming effects persist but are asymmetrical when primes are semantically implausible.
Priming strength increases with recency (proximity) and cumulative exposure to the prime structure.
The structural representations may encode hierarchical syntactic information, as shown by priming with nested dependencies.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on only two syntactic alternations in English.
The corpus is template-based and may not capture naturalistic language.
Only auto-regressive language models are considered; masked LMs are not investigated.
future_direction: Extend the investigation to other syntactic constructions and languages.
Use more naturalistic data beyond template-based corpora.
Investigate structural priming in masked language models.
papers.abstract: Abstract We investigate the extent to which modern neural language models are susceptible to structural priming, the phenomenon whereby the structure of a sentence makes the same structure more probable in a follow-up sentence. We explore how priming can be used to study the potential of these models to learn abstract structural information, which is a prerequisite for good performance on tasks that require natural language understanding skills. We introduce a novel metric and release Prime-LM, a large corpus where we control for various linguistic factors that interact with priming strength. We find that Transformer models indeed show evidence of structural priming, but also that the generalizations they learned are to some extent modulated by semantic information. Our experiments also show that the representations acquired by the models may not only encode abstract sequential structure but involve certain level of hierarchical syntactic information. More generally, our study shows that the priming paradigm is a useful, additional tool for gaining insights into the capacities of language models and opens the door to future priming-based investigations that probe the model’s internal states.1

papers.title: How Syntax Specialization Emerges in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does syntactic specialization emerge and evolve over training, and how do model initialization, scale, and training data shape this development?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Syntactic Sensitivity Index (SSI) to measure syntactic specialization in language models, revealing that syntactic sensitivity emerges gradually, concentrates in specific layers, exhibits a critical period, and is consistent across architectures but implemented by different neurons.
papers.conclusion: Provides the first systematic, mechanistic account of how syntactic specialization emerges in transformer language models by introducing SSI and applying it across training trajectories, seeds, and model scales, offering an integrated picture of when, where, and how syntax is represented.
papers.key_findings:
SSI correlates with grammaticality judgment accuracy and outperforms supervised probing methods like SVM and regression.
Syntactic specialization emerges gradually during training, with different syntactic phenomena showing distinct acquisition timelines and layer profiles.
There is a critical period (around 16 million tokens) during which syntactic specialization rapidly emerges and then stabilizes.
While layer-level syntactic representations converge across different random seeds, the specific neurons responsible for syntax sensitivity differ (convergent layers, divergent neurons).
Larger models and more training data enhance syntactic abstraction and specialization, but the effect varies across syntactic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Relies on sentence embeddings (mean pooling) which may miss token-level nuance or positional dynamics.
BLiMP focuses on binary acceptability, leaving gradient judgments, semantic-pragmatic interactions, and multi-sentence structures underexplored.
Open theoretical questions about minimal inductive bias, architectural interventions, and relation to semantic grounding.
future_direction: Extend SSI to token-level activations or attention maps.
Explore gradient judgments, semantic-pragmatic interactions, and multi-sentence structures beyond binary acceptability.
Investigate the minimal inductive bias or data regime required for syntactic specialization, architectural interventions, and how syntactic development relates to semantic grounding.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been found to develop surprising internal specializations: Individual neurons, attention heads, and circuits become selectively sensitive to syntactic structure, reflecting patterns observed in the human brain. While this specialization is well-documented, how it emerges during training and what influences its development remains largely unknown. In this work, we tap into the black box of specialization by tracking its formation over time. By quantifying internal syntactic consistency across minimal pairs from various syntactic phenomena, we identify a clear developmental trajectory: Syntactic sensitivity emerges gradually, concentrates in specific layers, and exhibits a 'critical period' of rapid internal specialization. This process is consistent across architectures and initialization parameters (e.g., random seeds), and is influenced by model scale and training data. We therefore reveal not only where syntax arises in LLMs but also how some models internalize it during training. To support future research, we will release the code, models, and training checkpoints upon acceptance.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Does syntax need to grow on trees? Sources of hierarchical inductive\n bias in sequence-to-sequence networks
papers.research_question: Which architectural factors affect the generalization behavior of neural sequence-to-sequence models trained on two syntactic tasks, English question formation and English tense reinflection?
papers.core_contribution: Only tree-structured models given correct parse trees consistently displayed a hierarchical bias across syntactic tasks, suggesting that human-like syntactic generalization requires architectural syntactic structure.
papers.conclusion: Many architectural factors can affect inductive biases, but a consistent hierarchical bias across syntactic tasks only emerges in models with explicit tree structure and correct parse information, suggesting that human-like syntactic generalization may require such structure when learning from text alone.
papers.key_findings:
The type of recurrent unit and attention qualitatively affect inductive biases, with interactions between them.
LSTMs and GRUs have different inductive biases, partly due to squashing in GRUs.
Only tree-based models with correct parse trees consistently generalized hierarchically across both question formation and tense reinflection.
Sequential models failed to generalize hierarchically even when given bracketed input or in multi-task learning settings.
Tree-based models are not constrained to hierarchical generalizations and can learn linear transformations if trained on unambiguous data.
papers.limitation:
The training data omits many cues available to children, such as prosody and real-world grounding, which may affect generalization.
Multi-task learning had limited effect in imparting hierarchical bias, suggesting that neural networks may not readily transfer knowledge across tasks.
future_direction: Investigating how to effectively use tree-based models without providing correct parses.
Characterizing the effects of hyperparameters and random seeds on generalization.
papers.abstract:
Learners that are exposed to the same training data might generalize
differently due to differing inductive biases. In neural network models,
inductive biases could in theory arise from any aspect of the model
architecture. We investigate which architectural factors affect the
generalization behavior of neural sequence-to-sequence models trained on two
syntactic tasks, English question formation and English tense reinflection. For
both tasks, the training set is consistent with a generalization based on
hierarchical structure and a generalization based on linear order. All
architectural factors that we investigated qualitatively affected how models
generalized, including factors with no clear connection to hierarchical
structure. For example, LSTMs and GRUs displayed qualitatively different
inductive biases. However, the only factor that consistently contributed a
hierarchical bias across tasks was the use of a tree-structured model rather
than a model with sequential recurrence, suggesting that human-like syntactic
generalization requires architectural syntactic structure.

papers.title: ParaScopes: What do Language Models Activations Encode About Future Text?
papers.research_question: Does a language model encode information about its likely future outputs within its internal representations? This is operationalized as the planningDecodability Hypothesis.
