papers.core_contribution: Introduces ParaScopes, a framework of Residual Stream Decoders, and provides evidence that language models encode paragraph-scale planning information in their activations, decodable with a lookahead of about 5 tokens.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that language models encode paragraph-scale planning information in their activations, which can be partially decoded using ParaScopes, with planning signals concentrated in middle layers and updated at paragraph boundaries.
papers.key_findings:
Paragraph-level planning information is decodable from residual stream activations, comparable to having 5-10 tokens of lookahead.
TAE ParaScope captures broad semantic signals (topic/subject), while Continuation ParaScope is more inconsistent but can sometimes reveal more specific details.
Planning signals are concentrated in the middle layers (approximately 60-80% of the model's depth).
Models update plans just-in-time at paragraph boundaries, with a sharp shift in information at the '\n\n' token.
Outline-level planning is weakly decodable, suggesting limited planning at longer horizons in the studied model.
papers.limitation:
The planning signals extracted may not be strictly causal to model performance.
Focus on short structured paragraphs and outlines, which may not generalize to domains like math, code, and chemistry.
Tests are primarily limited to one model (Llama 3.2 3B).
future_direction: Further research into understanding the degree to which the planning signals are strictly causal to model performance.
Extend the approach to different horizons and investigate how these mechanisms interact with factual correctness or stylistic consistency.
Investigate planning in models of various sizes.
papers.abstract: Interpretability studies in language models often investigate forward-looking representations of activations. However, as language models become capable of doing ever longer time horizon tasks, methods for understanding activations often remain limited to testing specific concepts or tokens. We develop a framework of Residual Stream Decoders as a method of probing model activations for paragraph-scale and document-scale plans. We test several methods and find information can be decoded equivalent to 5+ tokens of future context in small models. These results lay the groundwork for better monitoring of language models and better understanding how they might encode longer-term planning information.

papers.title: Incremental Processing of Principle B: Mismatches Between Neural Models and Humans
papers.research_question: Do GPT-based autoregressive neural language models use Principle B to restrict their incremental coreference processing like humans? Specifically, does Principle B block the influence of ungrammatical structural positions on pronoun prediction and cataphoric processing?
papers.core_contribution: GPT-based language models do not categorically ignore structural positions blocked by Principle B during incremental coreference processing, unlike humans. This mismatch suggests that certain aspects of human parsing behavior are not directly evidenced in linguistic data and may relate to properties of the training data.
papers.conclusion: Autoregressive neural models do not uniformly process pronouns like humans; they fail to capture qualitative patterns of incremental coreference processing and underestimate processing costs. Models appear to learn only those aspects of Principle B that have predictable reflexes in training data.
papers.key_findings:
For object pronouns (him) in positions where Principle B blocks co-indexation, all models exhibited a negative Gender Mismatch Effect (GMME), meaning they expected the pronoun to mismatch in gender with the grammatically unavailable antecedent.
For possessive pronouns (his), all models showed positive GMMEs across all structural positions, expecting gender agreement with antecedents.
In cataphoric object pronoun processing, larger models (GPT-J and GPT-3) showed no significant GMME when Principle B blocked coreference, aligning with human behavior, while smaller models (GPT-2 XL and GPT-Neo) showed a positive GMME.
Neural models greatly underestimate the magnitude of processing costs observed in humans, even in cases of qualitative overlap.
Analysis of the training data (the Pile) reveals a surface distribution bias where pronouns are more likely to mismatch in gender with antecedents in positions blocked by Principle B, suggesting models may overfit this pattern.
papers.limitation:
Whether models truly 'interpret' the correct coreference relations is unclear; techniques are limited for assessing if models comprehend meaning in a human-like fashion.
The study relies on stereotypical associations between nouns and pronouns, which does not cleanly map onto the real world (e.g., singular they is not considered).
The investigation is limited to English, due to resource availability and the focus of existing psycholinguistic work, limiting generalizability.
future_direction: Future work might consider analyses of the attention mechanisms to dig deeper into what information models are using.
papers.abstract: Despite neural language models qualitatively capturing many human linguistic behaviors, recent work has demonstrated that they underestimate the true processing costs of ungrammatical structures. We extend these more fine-grained comparisons between humans and models by investigating the interaction between Principle B and coreference processing. While humans use Principle B to block certain structural positions from affecting their incremental processing, we find that GPT-based language models are influenced by ungrammatical positions. We conclude by relating the mismatch between neural models and humans to properties of training data and suggest that certain aspects of human processing behavior do not directly follow from linguistic data.Paper at CoNLL 2022

papers.title: Using Priming to Uncover the Organization of Syntactic Representations\n in Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How are syntactic representations organized in neural language models? The paper investigates the organization of representations for sentences with relative clauses using a priming-based technique.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel technique based on syntactic priming to analyze how syntactic representations are organized in neural language models, and demonstrates that LSTM LMs' representations of sentences with relative clauses are organized hierarchically in a linguistically interpretable manner.
papers.conclusion: The proposed priming-based technique reveals that the representations of sentences with relative clauses in LSTM LMs are organized in a linguistically interpretable hierarchical manner.
papers.key_findings:
Sentences with the same syntactic structure are more similar to each other in the LM's representation space than lexically matched sentences with different structures.
Sentences with different types of relative clauses are more similar to each other than to sentences without relative clauses, suggesting LMs track the abstract property of a gap.
LMs track linguistically interpretable features like reduction and passivity, with passivity contributing more to similarity than reduction.
Similarity between sentences is driven not only by shared function words but also by abstract syntactic properties, though this ability decreases with increased training corpus size.
No evidence was found that the similarity between object RCs and other RCs predicts agreement prediction accuracy.
papers.limitation:
For linguistically interpretable classes without lexically observable properties, similarity might be driven by lexical items rather than abstract properties.
No evidence found that similarity between object RCs and other RCs predicts agreement prediction accuracy.
future_direction: Compare similarity matrices generated from LMs with human representations using priming experiments.
Explore how to bias models to track linguistically useful properties through architectural biases, training on auxiliary tasks, or data augmentation.
papers.abstract:
Neural language models (LMs) perform well on tasks that require sensitivity
to syntactic structure. Drawing on the syntactic priming paradigm from
psycholinguistics, we propose a novel technique to analyze the representations
that enable such success. By establishing a gradient similarity metric between
structures, this technique allows us to reconstruct the organization of the
LMs' syntactic representational space. We use this technique to demonstrate
that LSTM LMs' representations of different types of sentences with relative
clauses are organized hierarchically in a linguistically interpretable manner,
suggesting that the LMs track abstract properties of the sentence.

papers.title: Incremental Sentence Processing Mechanisms in Autoregressive Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether LMs use syntactic features or shallow heuristics for incremental sentence processing, if they represent only one or multiple interpretations simultaneously, and if they reanalyze or repair initial incorrect representations upon disambiguating evidence.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that LMs use both syntactic features and heuristics for garden path sentence processing, represent multiple interpretations simultaneously, and do not re-use features for follow-up questions.
papers.conclusion: LMs incrementally process sentences using a mix of syntactic and heuristic features, hold multiple interpretations, but do not re-use these features for downstream tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Many important features used by LMs are interpretable and syntax-related, but some are uninterpretable or spurious heuristics.
LMs' representations encode multiple interpretations of garden path sentences simultaneously.
LMs do not reanalyze or repair initial structural predictions upon disambiguating evidence.
Features identified are causally relevant to model behavior, as shown by interventions.
LMs do not re-use features from garden path processing to answer follow-up reading comprehension questions.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to specific models (Pythia-70m and Gemma-2-2b) and garden path sentences; results could be strengthened by extending to more diverse models and architectures.
future_direction: Extend analysis to models with more diverse training setups, scales, and architectures.
Investigate incremental sentence processing in more typical partial sentences to see if different mechanisms are used.
papers.abstract: Autoregressive transformer language models (LMs) possess strong syntactic abilities, often successfully handling phenomena from agreement to NPI licensing. However, the features they use to incrementally process language inputs are not well understood. In this paper, we fill this gap by studying the mechanisms underlying garden path sentence processing in LMs. We ask: (1) Do LMs use syntactic features or shallow heuristics to perform incremental sentence processing? (2) Do LMs represent only one potential interpretation, or multiple? and (3) Do LMs reanalyze or repair their initial incorrect representations? To address these questions, we use sparse autoencoders to identify interpretable features that determine which continuation - and thus which reading - of a garden path sentence the LM prefers. We find that while many important features relate to syntactic structure, some reflect syntactically irrelevant heuristics. Moreover, while most active features correspond to one reading of the sentence, some features correspond to the other, suggesting that LMs assign weight to both possibilities simultaneously. Finally, LMs do not re-use features from garden path sentence processing to answer follow-up questions.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: Language Models as Models of Language
papers.research_question: What can modern language models contribute to theoretical linguistics, particularly regarding language acquisition and competence?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that language models, when trained on developmentally plausible data and tested with controlled experiments, can serve as testbeds for evaluating linguistic hypotheses and inform debates about linguistic nativism.
papers.conclusion: Closer collaboration between theoretical linguists and computational researchers could yield valuable insights, particularly in advancing debates about linguistic nativism.
papers.key_findings:
Language models can learn hierarchical syntactic structure from exposure to data.
Language models exhibit sensitivity to various linguistic phenomena, even with developmentally plausible amounts of data.
Language models have inductive biases that favor natural language structures over impossible languages.
Language models can be used to test learnability claims and challenge strong nativist positions.
Causal intervention methods can help uncover the mechanisms by which language models process syntax.
papers.limitation: There is a large discrepancy between the amount of data used to train state-of-the-art language models and the data available to children during language acquisition.
future_direction: Using language models trained on developmentally plausible data (e.g., the BabyLM challenge).
Employing causal intervention methods to better understand model mechanisms.
Fostering closer collaboration between theoretical linguists and computational researchers.
papers.abstract: This chapter critically examines the potential contributions of modern language models to theoretical linguistics. Despite their focus on engineering goals, these models' ability to acquire sophisticated linguistic knowledge from mere exposure to data warrants a careful reassessment of their relevance to linguistic theory. I review a growing body of empirical evidence suggesting that language models can learn hierarchical syntactic structure and exhibit sensitivity to various linguistic phenomena, even when trained on developmentally plausible amounts of data. While the competence/performance distinction has been invoked to dismiss the relevance of such models to linguistic theory, I argue that this assessment may be premature. By carefully controlling learning conditions and making use of causal intervention methods, experiments with language models can potentially constrain hypotheses about language acquisition and competence. I conclude that closer collaboration between theoretical linguists and computational researchers could yield valuable insights, particularly in advancing debates about linguistic nativism.

papers.title: Linguistically Grounded Analysis of Language Models using Shapley Head Values
papers.research_question: How is linguistic knowledge, specifically morphosyntactic phenomena, encoded and processed in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Shapley Head Value (SHV) attributions can identify subnetworks in language models that correspond to linguistic phenomena, supporting the hypothesis that models learn linguistically grounded internal structures.
papers.conclusion: SHV-based attributions can identify attention heads of subnetworks that generalize across related morphosyntactic phenomena, enabling linguistically grounded analysis of language models.
papers.key_findings:
Clusters of BLiMP paradigms based on SHVs show consistency across BERT and RoBERTa models.
Clusters often group paradigms from the same linguistic category, indicating models organize knowledge by linguistic phenomena.
Pruning analysis shows linguistic knowledge is often localized in specific attention heads.
RoBERTa is more discerning than BERT in separating linguistic phenomena, likely due to more pretraining data and parameters.
SHVs are useful for identifying subnetworks that generalize across related morphosyntactic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Difficulty scaling to new languages and models due to lack of datasets and need for manual linguistic analysis.
BLiMP sentences are semantically empty and formulaic, though this is balanced between grammatical and ungrammatical examples.
SHV derivation uses sampling and heuristics, introducing uncertainty in attribution accuracy.
Binary gates for pruning may cause out-of-distribution issues, making it hard to disentangle head importance from ablation impact.
Attribution at the attention head level loses granularity compared to neuron-level analysis.
future_direction: Applying the methods to cross-lingual settings to describe subnetworks specific to linguistic knowledge in language models.
papers.abstract: Understanding how linguistic knowledge is encoded in language models is crucial for improving their generalisation capabilities. In this paper, we investigate the processing of morphosyntactic phenomena, by leveraging a recently proposed method for probing language models via Shapley Head Values (SHVs). Using the English language BLiMP dataset, we test our approach on two widely used models, BERT and RoBERTa, and compare how linguistic constructions such as anaphor agreement and filler-gap dependencies are handled. Through quantitative pruning and qualitative clustering analysis, we demonstrate that attention heads responsible for processing related linguistic phenomena cluster together. Our results show that SHV-based attributions reveal distinct patterns across both models, providing insights into how language models organize and process linguistic information. These findings support the hypothesis that language models learn subnetworks corresponding to linguistic theory, with potential implications for cross-linguistic model analysis and interpretability in Natural Language Processing (NLP).

papers.title: Syntactic Perturbations Reveal Representational Correlates of\n Hierarchical Phrase Structure in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: What aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by pretrained language model representations, and how are they built along the stacked layers of the network?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interventional, input perturbation-based analysis method to show that Transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, with larger contexts and more complex phrase boundaries becoming more salient in deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: Transformers build sensitivity to larger parts of the sentence along their layers, and hierarchical phrase structure plays a role in this process; structured input perturbations are a useful tool for analyzing deep networks.
papers.key_findings:
Representations are more distorted by shuffling small n-grams in early layers and by large n-grams in later layers, indicating increasing characteristic scale of context along layers.
Swapping two constituent phrases causes less distortion than swapping non-phrase spans of the same length, indicating sensitivity to phrase structure.
Swapping adjacent words across phrase boundaries causes more distortion than within boundaries, and distortion increases with syntactic distance, indicating sensitivity to phrase hierarchy.
Changes in attention weights partially explain the sensitivity to syntactic distance, with deeper layers showing more correlation.
The observed sensitivities are not due to simple co-occurrence statistics, as shown by controlling for PMI.
future_direction: Developing a formal theory of efficient hierarchical data representations in distributed features
Searching for the causal connection between attention structure, representational geometry, and model performance
Exploring applications in network pruning studies
Extending the method as a hypothesis generator in neuroscience to understand compositional structure in neural populations
papers.abstract:
While vector-based language representations from pretrained language models
have set a new standard for many NLP tasks, there is not yet a complete
accounting of their inner workings. In particular, it is not entirely clear
what aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by these representations,
nor how (if at all) they are built along the stacked layers of the network. In
this paper, we aim to address such questions with a general class of
interventional, input perturbation-based analyses of representations from
pretrained language models. Importing from computational and cognitive
neuroscience the notion of representational invariance, we perform a series of
probes designed to test the sensitivity of these representations to several
kinds of structure in sentences. Each probe involves swapping words in a
sentence and comparing the representations from perturbed sentences against the
original. We experiment with three different perturbations: (1) random
permutations of n-grams of varying width, to test the scale at which a
representation is sensitive to word position; (2) swapping of two spans which
do or do not form a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to global phrase
structure; and (3) swapping of two adjacent words which do or do not break
apart a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to local phrase structure.
 Results from these probes collectively suggest that Transformers build
sensitivity to larger parts of the sentence along their layers, and that
hierarchical phrase structure plays a role in this process. More broadly, our
results also indicate that structured input perturbations widens the scope of
analyses that can be performed on often-opaque deep learning systems, and can
serve as a complement to existing tools (such as supervised linear probes) for
interpreting complex black-box models.

papers.title: Shadow of the (Hierarchical) Tree: Reconciling Symbolic and Predictive Components of the Neural Code for Syntax
papers.research_question: How can symbolic representations and connectionist neural networks be integrated to account for both hierarchical (vertical) and linear/predictive (horizontal) aspects of natural language syntax?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a hybrid neurosymbolic model that reconciles symbolic hierarchical syntax and connectionist linear/predictive processes via oscillatory phase codes, specifically extending the ROSE architecture.
papers.conclusion: A hybrid neurosymbolic approach, using oscillatory phase codes, can reconcile symbolic and predictive components of syntax, providing a path forward for cognitive neuroscience and language modeling.
papers.key_findings:
The ROSE architecture provides a symbolic account of hierarchical syntax via oscillatory mechanisms like phase-amplitude coupling.
Horizontal syntactic information (linear, statistical) can be integrated via predictive coding and statistical inference at lower levels of ROSE.
Oscillatory phase codes (e.g., traveling waves modulating high-frequency spiking) provide a feasible interface between symbolic and statistical representations.
Large language models (LLMs) are more competent at modeling horizontal syntactic information than vertical hierarchical syntax, indicating a limitation in their compositional reasoning.
A mathematical model demonstrates how frontotemporal traveling waves can dynamically modulate high-frequency spiking activity to integrate symbolic and statistical information for morphosyntax.
future_direction: Integrating associationist and predictive neural mechanisms into the existing ROSE architecture.
Mathematical formalization of the ROSE architecture and its hybrid extensions.
Testing the proposed hybrid neurosymbolic model with empirical neural data.
papers.abstract: Natural language syntax can serve as a major test for how to integrate two infamously distinct frameworks: symbolic representations and connectionist neural networks. Building on a recent neurocomputational architecture for syntax (ROSE), I discuss the prospects of reconciling the neural code for hierarchical 'vertical' syntax with linear and predictive 'horizontal' processes via a hybrid neurosymbolic model. I argue that the former can be accounted for via the higher levels of ROSE in terms of vertical phrase structure representations, while the latter can explain horizontal forms of linguistic information via the tuning of the lower levels to statistical and perceptual inferences. One prediction of this is that artificial language models will contribute to the cognitive neuroscience of horizontal morphosyntax, but much less so to hierarchically compositional structures. I claim that this perspective helps resolve many current tensions in the literature. Options for integrating these two neural codes are discussed, with particular emphasis on how predictive coding mechanisms can serve as interfaces between symbolic oscillatory phase codes and population codes for the statistics of linearized aspects of syntax. Lastly, I provide a neurosymbolic mathematical model for how to inject symbolic representations into a neural regime encoding lexico-semantic statistical features.

papers.title: Inferring the nature of linguistic computations in the brain
papers.research_question: How can we infer the nature of linguistic computations from neural data, and what are the pitfalls in interpreting such data and models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that neural data alone is insufficient to infer the computational mechanisms of sentence processing, and that models must be evaluated based on cognitive, neural, and linguistic principles to be explanatory.
papers.conclusion: Computational modeling is vital for understanding sentence processing, but models must compute linguistically-sufficient representations via explicit cognitive operations and stay faithful to neurophysiological principles, and should not be judged solely on predictive power.
papers.key_findings:
The presence of a 1-2-4 Hz pattern in neural data does not necessarily imply hierarchical processing; it can also arise from associative models.
Artificial neural networks can produce the 1-2-4 Hz pattern without explicit sentence structure, but this does not rule out hierarchical processing in the brain.
Predictive power of a model is not the sole criterion for explaining brain function; models must also be faithful to cognitive and neural principles.
The amount of training data used in ANNs may not reflect the brain's learning environment, and rule-based models might be more explanatory in some cases.
Statistical models are not necessarily more parsimonious than hierarchical models, as they may require extensive training and latent syntactic information.
future_direction: Using naturalistic paradigms to study language processing
Integrating multiple data sources (e.g., EEG, fMRI) to test models
Developing models that are explicit about cognitive operations and neurophysiological implementation
papers.abstract: Sentences contain structure that determines their meaning beyond that of individual words. An influential study by Ding and colleagues (2016) used frequency tagging of phrases and sentences to show that the human brain is sensitive to structure by finding peaks of neural power at the rate at which structures were presented. Since then, there has been a rich debate on how to best explain this pattern of results with profound impact on the language sciences. Models that use hierarchical structure building, as well as models based on associative sequence processing, can predict the neural response, creating an inferential impasse as to which class of models explains the nature of the linguistic computations reflected in the neural readout. In the current manuscript, we discuss pitfalls and common fallacies seen in the conclusions drawn in the literature illustrated by various simulations. We conclude that inferring the neural operations of sentence processing based on these neural data, and any like it, alone, is insufficient. We discuss how to best evaluate models and how to approach the modeling of neural readouts to sentence processing in a manner that remains faithful to cognitive, neural, and linguistic principles.

papers.title: Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Mechanisms in Neural Language\n Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind syntactic agreement in neural language models, specifically how do models prefer grammatical inflections and do neurons process agreement similarly across different syntactic structures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that language models use two distinct mechanisms for subject-verb agreement depending on whether the subject and verb are adjacent, and that larger models do not necessarily learn stronger preferences.
papers.conclusion: The study applies causal mediation analysis to reveal mechanisms behind syntactic agreement in pre-trained language models, showing how neurons are implicated and providing insights into model inner workings.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-2 and Transformer-XL use two distinct mechanisms for subject-verb agreement: one for adjacent subject-verb pairs and another for non-adjacent pairs, while XLNet uses a unified mechanism.
Larger models have more distributed agreement mechanisms across layers, but do not always have stronger preferences for correct inflections.
The overlap of high-NIE neurons across syntactic structures correlates with human intuitions of syntactic similarity.
Plural subjects consistently have higher grammaticality values than singular subjects across structures.
Adverbial distractors increase the probability of correct verb inflections more than incorrect ones, while attractors decrease total effects.
future_direction: Intervening on groups of neurons and attention heads to see how components work together
Extending the analysis to phenomena such as filler-gap dependencies and negative polarity items
Examining the impact of specific verbs on syntactic agreement mechanisms
papers.abstract:
Targeted syntactic evaluations have demonstrated the ability of language
models to perform subject-verb agreement given difficult contexts. To elucidate
the mechanisms by which the models accomplish this behavior, this study applies
causal mediation analysis to pre-trained neural language models. We investigate
the magnitude of models' preferences for grammatical inflections, as well as
whether neurons process subject-verb agreement similarly across sentences with
different syntactic structures. We uncover similarities and differences across
architectures and model sizes -- notably, that larger models do not necessarily
learn stronger preferences. We also observe two distinct mechanisms for
producing subject-verb agreement depending on the syntactic structure of the
input sentence. Finally, we find that language models rely on similar sets of
neurons when given sentences with similar syntactic structure.

papers.title: Improving Reasoning Performance in Large Language Models via Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: Can reasoning performance in LLMs be improved by applying control vectors derived from model activations to the residual stream during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Reasoning performance in LLMs can be improved by applying control vectors derived from model activations to the residual stream during inference, without any additional training.
papers.conclusion: The experiments indicate that reasoning can in part be understood to be encoded in the residual stream, similarly to how emotional valence or other features are encoded, and can be modulated via representation engineering.
papers.key_findings:
Control vectors derived from contrastive pairs or PCA can improve model performance on inductive, deductive, and mathematical reasoning tasks.
The intervention generalizes across tasks: control vectors from bAbI improve GSM8K performance and vice versa.
The intervention changes the model's internal representations, as evidenced by changes in KL divergence and entropy.
The method requires no additional training and works by adding control vectors to the residual stream during inference.
The optimal scaling factor α varies across models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Limited scope of models (smaller than production-level state-of-the-art models).
The IOI task is relatively simple, which limits the scope of potential errors and the generalizability of findings.
The need for better contrastive pairs for reasoning to optimally derive control vectors.
future_direction: Applying the intervention to much larger models.
Applying the intervention to more general tasks.
Testing different contrastive schemes.
Exploring ways of embedding this methodology into the models.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have resulted in increasingly anthropomorphic language concerning the ability of LLMs to reason. Whether reasoning in LLMs should be understood to be inherently different is, however, widely debated. We propose utilizing a representation engineering approach wherein model activations are read from the residual stream of an LLM when processing a reasoning task. The activations are used to derive a control vector that is applied to the model as an inference-time intervention, modulating the representational space of the model, to improve performance on the specified task. We publish the code for deriving control vectors and analyzing model representations. The method allows us to improve performance on reasoning benchmarks and assess how control vectors influence the final logit distribution of a model via metrics such as KL divergence and entropy. We apply control vectors to Mistral-7B-Instruct and a range of Pythia models on an inductive, a deductive and mathematical reasoning task. We show that an LLM can, to a certain degree, be controlled to improve its perceived reasoning ability by modulating activations. The intervention is dependent upon the ability to reliably extract the model's typical state when correctly solving a task. Our results suggest that reasoning performance can be modulated in the same manner as other information-processing tasks performed by LLMs and demonstrate that we are capable of improving performance on specific tasks via a simple intervention on the residual stream with no additional training.

papers.title: Different types of syntactic agreement recruit the same units within large language models
papers.research_question: We investigate whether different syntactic phenomena recruit shared or distinct components in LLMs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that syntactic agreement phenomena recruit overlapping units in large language models, suggesting that agreement forms a functional category, and this pattern holds across languages with overlap correlating with syntactic similarity.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal that syntactic agreement constitutes a meaningful category within LLMs' representational spaces, with shared units across agreement types and languages, organized by syntactic similarity.
papers.key_findings:
Syntax-responsive units are consistently identified across sentence instances for each syntactic phenomenon and causally support model performance.
Different types of syntactic agreement (e.g., subject-verb, anaphor, determiner-noun) recruit overlapping sets of units in English.
The overlap among agreement units is higher than with non-agreement phenomena, indicating agreement as a shared functional category.
This pattern replicates in Russian and Chinese, with agreement units showing cross-lingual overlap.
Cross-lingual unit overlap for subject-verb agreement increases with syntactic similarity across 57 languages.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on top-n% unit localization may overlook more distributed syntactic representations.
Analyses are primarily correlational, though causal involvement is demonstrated via ablation.
Focus on benchmarks comparing grammatical to ungrammatical sentences, which may not capture full grammatical knowledge.
future_direction: Apply the approach to other syntactic phenomena, including infrequent structures, ambiguities, and long-distance dependencies.
Extend experiments to other languages with BLiMP-like benchmarks, such as Dutch or Turkish.
Investigate the relationship between syntax and semantics in model representations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can reliably distinguish grammatical from ungrammatical sentences, but how grammatical knowledge is represented within the models remains an open question. We investigate whether different syntactic phenomena recruit shared or distinct components in LLMs. Using a functional localization approach inspired by cognitive neuroscience, we identify the LLM units most responsive to 67 English syntactic phenomena in seven open-weight models. These units are consistently recruited across sentences containing the phenomena and causally support the models' syntactic performance. Critically, different types of syntactic agreement (e.g., subject-verb, anaphor, determiner-noun) recruit overlapping sets of units, suggesting that agreement constitutes a meaningful functional category for LLMs. This pattern holds in English, Russian, and Chinese; and further, in a cross-lingual analysis of 57 diverse languages, structurally more similar languages share more units for subject-verb agreement. Taken together, these findings reveal that syntactic agreement-a critical marker of syntactic dependencies-constitutes a meaningful category within LLMs' representational spaces.

papers.title: Mitigating Content Effects on Reasoning in Language Models through Fine-Grained Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How can content biases in reasoning be mitigated through activation steering in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces K-CAST, a fine-grained conditional activation steering method that effectively reduces content biases in reasoning, improving formal reasoning accuracy by up to 15%.
papers.conclusion: Activation-level interventions offer a scalable inference-time strategy for enhancing the robustness of LLMs, contributing towards more systematic and unbiased reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive steering methods enable linear control over content biases in reasoning.
Static steering is insufficient to debias all tested models.
K-CAST reduces biases on unresponsive models, achieving up to 15% absolute improvement in formal reasoning accuracy.
Steering for content effects is robust to prompt variations and incurs minimal side effects on multilingual language modeling capabilities.
Steering vectors can partially generalize to different out-of-distribution reasoning tasks.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are performed on LLMs of up to 9 billion parameters due to computational constraints.
The study focuses mainly on synthetically generated tasks, which may not fully capture real-world applications.
future_direction: Applying the steering methodology to larger models.
Assessing how steering for content effect can impact real-world applications in critical domains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently demonstrate reasoning limitations, often conflating content plausibility (i.e., material inference) with logical validity (i.e., formal inference). This can result in biased inferences, where plausible arguments are incorrectly deemed logically valid or vice versa. Mitigating this limitation is critical, as it undermines the trustworthiness and generalizability of LLMs in applications that demand rigorous logical consistency. This paper investigates the problem of mitigating content biases on formal reasoning through activation steering. Specifically, we curate a controlled syllogistic reasoning dataset to disentangle formal validity from content plausibility. After localising the layers responsible for formal and material inference, we investigate contrastive activation steering methods for test-time interventions. An extensive empirical analysis on different LLMs reveals that contrastive steering consistently supports linear control over content biases. However, we observe that a static approach is insufficient for improving all the tested models. We then leverage the possibility to control content effects by dynamically determining the value of the steering parameters via fine-grained conditional methods. We found that conditional steering is effective on unresponsive models, achieving up to 15% absolute improvement in formal reasoning accuracy with a newly introduced kNN-based method (K-CAST). Finally, additional experiments reveal that steering for content effects is robust to prompt variations, incurs minimal side effects on language modeling capabilities, and can partially generalize to out-of-distribution reasoning tasks. Practically, this paper demonstrates that activation-level interventions can offer a scalable strategy for enhancing the robustness of LLMs, contributing towards more systematic and unbiased formal reasoning.

papers.title: Does injecting linguistic structure into language models lead to better alignment with brain recordings?
papers.research_question: Does injecting linguistic structure into language models lead to better alignment with brain recordings?
papers.core_contribution: Injecting linguistic structure bias into language models via guided attention during fine-tuning can improve alignment with brain recordings, particularly for word-level fMRI data.
papers.conclusion: Injecting linguistic structure bias through guided attention can improve brain decoding performance, with clearer benefits for finer-grained (word-level) analyses, and highlights the importance of controlling for domain effects.
papers.key_findings:
For the word-level Wehbe2014 fMRI dataset, guided attention models significantly outperform pretrained and domain-finetuned baselines in brain decoding.
For the sentence-level Pereira2018 dataset, improvements are more modest, with UD and DM guided attention models showing some improvement over the pretrained baseline.
Domain of the fine-tuning data is an important confound affecting brain alignment; simply fine-tuning on a different domain can reduce alignment.
Guided attention models perform better on subject-verb agreement syntactic probing tasks, with performance ranking corresponding to brain decoding scores.
Guided attention improves performance on a semantic tagging task for most semantic categories, especially discourse and temporal relations.
papers.limitation:
The fMRI data was recorded during passive reading without a specific task, which may limit the ability to uncover fine-grained patterns of linguistic structure.
Potential confounds such as domain, corpus size, and dependency length differences between the linguistic formalisms are not fully controlled for due to the lack of a common annotated corpus.
future_direction: Investigating brain alignment using continuous, naturalistic listening fMRI datasets.
Using a common annotated corpus for all formalisms to properly control for confounds like domain and corpus size.
papers.abstract: Neuroscientists evaluate deep neural networks for natural language processing as possible candidate models for how language is processed in the brain. These models are often trained without explicit linguistic supervision, but have been shown to learn some linguistic structure in the absence of such supervision (Manning et al., 2020), potentially questioning the relevance of symbolic linguistic theories in modeling such cognitive processes (Warstadt and Bowman, 2020). We evaluate across two fMRI datasets whether language models align better with brain recordings, if their attention is biased by annotations from syntactic or semantic formalisms. Using structure from dependency or minimal recursion semantic annotations, we find alignments improve significantly for one of the datasets. For another dataset, we see more mixed results. We present an extensive analysis of these results. Our proposed approach enables the evaluation of more targeted hypotheses about the composition of meaning in the brain, expanding the range of possible scientific inferences a neuroscientist could make, and opens up new opportunities for cross-pollination between computational neuroscience and linguistics.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Interpretation of Multi-Step Reasoning Capabilities of Language Models
papers.research_question: Do language models perform multi-step reasoning tasks by using a reasoning mechanism or by memorizing answers from pretraining?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MechanisticProbe, a probing method that recovers reasoning trees from attention patterns, providing evidence that LMs perform multi-step reasoning mechanistically.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that reasoning trees can often be detected from LM attention patterns, supporting the claim that LMs may reason mechanistically.
papers.key_findings:
MechanisticProbe can recover reasoning trees from attention patterns of GPT-2 and LLaMA for most examples.
LMs identify useful statements in bottom layers and perform reasoning steps in higher layers.
Pruning attention heads that contribute to reasoning tree detection degrades performance, indicating a causal role.
Higher probing scores correlate with higher model accuracy and robustness to noise.
Finetuned models show clearer reasoning patterns in attention than few-shot models.
papers.limitation:
The study considered fairly simple reasoning tasks.
The analysis averages over attention heads, but heads may have different functions, especially in shallow models.
The analysis is limited to single-token prediction tasks and does not cover chain-of-thought reasoning.
future_direction: Explore more challenging reasoning tasks.
Analyze reasoning in chain-of-thought prompting settings.
papers.abstract: Yifan Hou, Jiaoda Li, Yu Fei, Alessandro Stolfo, Wangchunshu Zhou, Guangtao Zeng, Antoine Bosselut, Mrinmaya Sachan. Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2023.

papers.title: Neural Language Models as Psycholinguistic Subjects: Representations of\n Syntactic State
papers.research_question: To what extent do neural network language models reflect incremental representations of syntactic state?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models show evidence of incremental syntactic state representation, but the quality of representation depends on model architecture and training data size.
papers.conclusion: Psycholinguistic methods provide a valuable lens for probing the internal representations of neural language models, and representation of coarse-grained syntactic structure requires either syntactic supervision or large data, while exploiting fine-grained lexical cues requires large data.
papers.key_findings:
All models show basic evidence of syntactic state representation in subordinate clauses and garden path effects.
Large LSTMs (GRNN and JRNN) and the RNNG show more fine-grained sensitivity to syntactic cues, such as verb transitivity and morphological form.
Only GRNN and the RNNG fully capture the proper behavior of subordinate clauses (no-matrix penalty effect).
Large LSTMs use verb argument structure and morphological cues to modulate garden path effects, while TinyLSTM and RNNG do not.
Syntactic state representations degrade with increasing intervening material in some models (GRNN and TinyLSTM) but not in others (JRNN and RNNG).
papers.abstract:
We deploy the methods of controlled psycholinguistic experimentation to shed
light on the extent to which the behavior of neural network language models
reflects incremental representations of syntactic state. To do so, we examine
model behavior on artificial sentences containing a variety of syntactically
complex structures. We test four models: two publicly available LSTM sequence
models of English (Jozefowicz et al., 2016; Gulordava et al., 2018) trained on
large datasets; an RNNG (Dyer et al., 2016) trained on a small, parsed dataset;
and an LSTM trained on the same small corpus as the RNNG. We find evidence that
the LSTMs trained on large datasets represent syntactic state over large spans
of text in a way that is comparable to the RNNG, while the LSTM trained on the
small dataset does not or does so only weakly.

papers.title: Reasoning Circuits in Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Syllogistic Inference
papers.research_question: How is content-independent syllogistic reasoning internalized in LMs during pre-training? Are content-independent mechanisms disentangled from world knowledge and belief biases? Does the core reasoning mechanism generalize across syllogistic schemes, model sizes, and architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a sufficient and necessary circuit for syllogistic reasoning involving middle-term suppression, showing that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms that are susceptible to contamination from world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn transferable reasoning mechanisms but such mechanisms are contaminated and suppressed by the world knowledge acquired during pre-training, indicating a lack of generalizable abstract logical primitives.
papers.key_findings:
The circuit for syllogistic reasoning involves a three-stage mechanism: long induction, duplication, suppression, and mover heads.
The circuit is necessary and sufficient for symbolic syllogistic reasoning.
The circuit transfers to non-symbolic arguments but is contaminated by belief biases, with additional attention heads encoding world knowledge.
The circuit generalizes across unconditionally valid syllogistic schemes where models achieve high accuracy.
The suppression mechanism pattern is compatible across different model families and sizes, though with increasing complexity in larger models.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is confined to specific syllogistic reasoning templates and does not consider more complex scenarios.
The experimentation is confined due to the intricate level of granularity and computational complexity required in circuit analysis.
future_direction: Further studies to understand how the discovered symbolic circuit can be effectively disentangled from world knowledge to enable systematic generalization in LMs’ reasoning.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on reasoning in language models (LMs) have sparked a debate on whether they can learn systematic inferential principles or merely exploit superficial patterns in the training data. To understand and uncover the mechanisms adopted for formal reasoning in LMs, this paper presents a mechanistic interpretation of syllogistic inference. Specifically, we present a methodology for circuit discovery aimed at interpreting content-independent and formal reasoning mechanisms. Through two distinct intervention methods, we uncover a sufficient and necessary circuit involving middle-term suppression that elucidates how LMs transfer information to derive valid conclusions from premises. Furthermore, we investigate how belief biases manifest in syllogistic inference, finding evidence of partial contamination from additional attention heads responsible for encoding commonsense and contextualized knowledge. Finally, we explore the generalization of the discovered mechanisms across various syllogistic schemes, model sizes and architectures. The identified circuit is sufficient and necessary for syllogistic schemes on which the models achieve high accuracy (>60%), with compatible activation patterns across models of different families. Overall, our findings suggest that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms, but that, at the same time, such mechanisms do not involve generalizable and abstract logical primitives, being susceptible to contamination by the same world knowledge acquired during pre-training.

papers.title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining? Does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning rarely alters a model's underlying capabilities; instead, it typically learns a minimal 'wrapper' transformation on top of existing capabilities. These wrapped capabilities can be sample-efficiently revived via further fine-tuning on relevant tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily learns minimal wrapper transformations over existing model capabilities rather than creating or deleting them, which has implications for safety as wrappers can be easily removed or bypassed.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning alters pretraining capabilities by minimally transforming them via a learned 'wrapper'.
Wrappers are often extremely localized; pruning a few neurons can cause the model to revert to its pretraining capability.
Further fine-tuning on a subset of pretraining data leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the original capability.
When a weakly relevant pretraining capability is present, the model exploits spurious correlations in the fine-tuning data via the wrapper.
The presence and strength of a pretraining capability (influenced by its sampling probability during pretraining) significantly affects fine-tuning dynamics and wrapper formation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted primarily in synthetic, controlled settings (Tracr and PCFGs), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex and realistic tasks and models.
Investigating the societal implications of the findings, particularly regarding the safety of fine-tuned models.
Exploring whether the wrapper phenomenon generalizes to other model adaptation methods beyond standard fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has become the de facto strategy for developing both task-specific and general-purpose machine learning systems, including developing models that are safe to deploy. Despite its clear importance, there has been minimal work that explains how fine-tuning alters the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining: does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones? We address this question empirically in synthetic, controlled settings where we can use mechanistic interpretability tools (e.g., network pruning and probing) to understand how the model's underlying capabilities are changing. We perform an extensive analysis of the effects of fine-tuning in these settings, and show that: (i) fine-tuning rarely alters the underlying model capabilities; (ii) a minimal transformation, which we call a 'wrapper', is typically learned on top of the underlying model capabilities, creating the illusion that they have been modified; and (iii) further fine-tuning on a task where such hidden capabilities are relevant leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the capability, i.e., the model begins reusing these capability after only a few gradient steps. This indicates that practitioners can unintentionally remove a model's safety wrapper merely by fine-tuning it on a, e.g., superficially unrelated, downstream task. We additionally perform analysis on language models trained on the TinyStories dataset to support our claims in a more realistic setup.

papers.title: Linguistic Structure Induction from Language Models
papers.research_question: How can constituency and dependency syntactic structures be induced from language models in an unsupervised setting, and what are the challenges and potential improvements?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis provides a detailed analysis and extension of StructFormer, a model for unsupervised induction of constituency and dependency structures, including architectural modifications and evaluation on linguistic tasks via the BabyLM challenge.
papers.conclusion: The results of this thesis encourage further development in the direction of retrofitting transformer-based models to induce syntactic structures, supported by the relatively acceptable performance of StructFormer in different experimental settings and the highlighted limitations that require innovative solutions.
papers.key_findings:
Reproducing StructFormer shows it can induce syntactic structures with acceptable performance.
The parser network placed in middle layers (layers 2-5) improves perplexity, but with inconsistent parsing results.
Subword tokenization can be integrated into StructFormer, but evaluation requires mapping subwords to words.
Pretraining on the BabyLM dataset yields competitive performance in linguistic tasks compared to other BabyLM models.
The StructFormer architecture does not consistently outperform a vanilla transformer on linguistic tasks, indicating room for improvement.
papers.limitation: The evaluation scores reported in studies on syntactic structure induction are often too weak to prove that language models adhere to linguistic theories.
future_direction: Exploring more sophisticated methods for integrating syntactic information.
Extending the approach to other languages.
Improving the evaluation metrics for syntactic structure induction.
papers.abstract: Linear sequences of words are implicitly represented in our brains by hierarchical structures that organize the composition of words in sentences. Linguists formalize different frameworks to model this hierarchy; two of the most common syntactic frameworks are Constituency and Dependency. Constituency represents sentences as nested groups of phrases, while dependency represents a sentence by assigning relations between its words. Recently, the pursuit of intelligent machines has produced Language Models (LMs) capable of solving many language tasks with a human-level performance. Many studies now question whether LMs implicitly represent syntactic hierarchies. This thesis focuses on producing constituency and dependency structures from LMs in an unsupervised setting. I review the critical methods in this field and highlight a line of work that utilizes a numerical representation for binary constituency trees (Syntactic Distance). I present a detailed study on StructFormer (SF) (Shen et al., 2021), which retrofits a transformer encoder architecture with a parser network to produce constituency and dependency structures. I present six experiments to analyze and address this field's challenges; experiments include investigating the effect of repositioning the parser network within the SF architecture, evaluating subword-based induced trees, and benchmarking the models developed in the thesis experiments on linguistic tasks. Models benchmarking is performed by participating in the BabyLM challenge, published at CoNLL 2023 (Momen et al., 2023). The results of this thesis encourage further development in the direction of retrofitting transformer-based models to induce syntactic structures, supported by the acceptable performance of SF in different experimental settings and the observed limitations that require innovative solutions to advance the state of syntactic structure induction.

papers.title: Cognitive Mirrors: Exploring the Diverse Functional Roles of Attention Heads in LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in large language models specialize for different cognitive functions during complex reasoning tasks, and what are their properties and roles?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel interpretability framework and the CogQA dataset to analyze attention heads in LLMs, revealing that cognitive heads are sparse, functionally specialized, and hierarchically organized, and are crucial for reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a deeper understanding of LLM reasoning and suggests implications for model design, training, and fine-tuning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads exhibit functional specialization for specific cognitive functions (cognitive heads) and are sparse (only a small subset of heads are important for each function).
Cognitive heads are universal across different LLM architectures and model sizes.
Cognitive heads show layered functional organization, with different functions localizing to different layers (e.g., retrieval in middle layers, math in higher layers).
Cognitive heads exhibit functional clustering and hierarchical structure, where lower-level functions (e.g., retrieval) support higher-level reasoning.
Removing cognitive heads degrades performance on corresponding functions, while enhancing them improves reasoning accuracy, demonstrating their causal importance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance in a variety of tasks, but remain largely opaque in terms of their internal mechanisms. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial to improve their reasoning abilities. Drawing inspiration from the interplay between neural processes and human cognition, we propose a novel interpretability framework to systematically analyze the roles and behaviors of attention heads, which are key components of LLMs. We introduce CogQA, a dataset that decomposes complex questions into step-by-step subquestions with a chain-of-thought design, each associated with specific cognitive functions such as retrieval or logical reasoning. By applying a multi-class probing method, we identify the attention heads responsible for these functions. Our analysis across multiple LLM families reveals that attention heads exhibit functional specialization, characterized as cognitive heads. These cognitive heads exhibit several key properties: they are universally sparse, vary in number and distribution across different cognitive functions, and display interactive and hierarchical structures. We further show that cognitive heads play a vital role in reasoning tasks - removing them leads to performance degradation, while augmenting them enhances reasoning accuracy. These insights offer a deeper understanding of LLM reasoning and suggest important implications for model design, training, and fine-tuning strategies.

papers.title: Echoes of BERT: Do Modern Language Models Rediscover the Classical NLP Pipeline?
papers.research_question: How do modern language models encode linguistic structure, and do they rediscover the classical NLP pipeline observed in earlier models like BERT?
papers.core_contribution: Modern language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline, with lexical information concentrated in early layers and becoming nonlinear, while inflectional morphology remains linearly accessible across layers and languages.
papers.conclusion: Modern transformer language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline and exhibit robust representational regularities for lexical and inflectional information across architectures, sizes, and languages.
papers.key_findings:
Modern LMs consistently organize linguistic information hierarchically: early layers process syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entities, later layers capture discourse.
Lexical identity (lemma) information is most accessible in early layers and becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network.
Inflectional morphology remains highly linearly accessible across all layers and across six typologically diverse languages.
These representational patterns emerge early during pretraining and are robust across model architectures, sizes, and training regimes.
Inflectional features occupy compact, linearly accessible subspaces in the residual stream, enabling effective steering interventions.
papers.limitation:
Representation extraction for decoder-only models uses the final subword token, which may not be optimal for all architectures.
The study does not explicitly examine cases where different grammatical functions share the same surface form (e.g., infinitive and non-past verb forms).
Classifiers only detect correlations in hidden activations, not causal mechanisms.
Steering experiments measure changes in classifier performance rather than downstream model outputs.
future_direction: Develop better extraction methods for word representations from decoder-only models.
Examine how models separate form from function across languages in cases of surface-form ambiguity.
Design more complex experiments to evaluate steering effects on actual model generation.
papers.abstract: Large transformer-based language models dominate modern NLP, yet our understanding of how they encode linguistic information relies primarily on studies of early models like BERT and GPT-2. Building on classic BERTology work, we analyze 25 models spanning from classical architectures (BERT, DeBERTa, GPT-2) to modern large language models (Pythia, OLMo-2, Gemma-2, Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1), probing layer-by-layer representations across eight linguistic tasks in English. Consistent with earlier findings, we find that hierarchical organization persists in modern models: early layers capture syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entity-level information, and later layers encode discourse phenomena. We dive deeper, conducting an in-depth multilingual analysis of two specific linguistic properties - lexical identity and inflectional morphology - that help disentangle form from meaning. We find that lexical information concentrates linearly in early layers but becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network, while inflectional information remains linearly accessible throughout all layers. Additional analyses of attention mechanisms, steering vectors, and pretraining checkpoints reveal where this information resides within layers, how it can be functionally manipulated, and how representations evolve during pretraining. Taken together, our findings suggest that, even with substantial advances in LLM technologies, transformer models learn to organize linguistic information in similar ways, regardless of model architecture, size, or training regime, indicating that these properties are important for next token prediction. Our code is available at https://github.com/ml5885/model_internal_sleuthing

papers.title: Analysing Neural Language Models: Contextual Decomposition Reveals\n Default Reasoning in Number and Gender Assignment
papers.research_question: How do neural language models (specifically LSTMs) process grammatical phenomena such as number agreement and gender anaphora resolution? What information do they base their decisions on, and do they exhibit default reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Generalised Contextual Decomposition (GCD), a method to decompose LSTM predictions into contributions from input phrases and model biases, and uses it to reveal that LSTM language models employ default reasoning for number and gender assignment, with singular and masculine as defaults encoded in the model weights.
papers.conclusion: GCD is a powerful method for analyzing LSTM language models, revealing default reasoning in number and gender assignment, and can be extended to other models and improved with better Shapley value approximations.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM language models exhibit a default reasoning effect: singular and masculine are default categories hard-coded in the model weights.
For number agreement, plural verb predictions depend strongly on the subject, while singular verb predictions rely more on other sentence elements and model intercepts.
For gender anaphora, the model has a male default bias; predicting female pronouns requires explicit evidence from female referents.
The model shows gender bias in stereotypical gender roles: male-stereotyped job titles lead to male pronoun preference, but female-stereotyped job titles do not lead to a female preference.
GCD enables detailed analysis of anaphora resolution in language models, pinpointing where and how resolution takes place.
future_direction: Extending GCD to attention-based models
Improving the gate factorisation with better Shapley value approximators
Exploring the axiomatic approach to relate GCD to other explanation methods
papers.abstract:
Extensive research has recently shown that recurrent neural language models
are able to process a wide range of grammatical phenomena. How these models are
able to perform these remarkable feats so well, however, is still an open
question. To gain more insight into what information LSTMs base their decisions
on, we propose a generalisation of Contextual Decomposition (GCD). In
particular, this setup enables us to accurately distil which part of a
prediction stems from semantic heuristics, which part truly emanates from
syntactic cues and which part arise from the model biases themselves instead.
We investigate this technique on tasks pertaining to syntactic agreement and
co-reference resolution and discover that the model strongly relies on a
default reasoning effect to perform these tasks.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: Word-order Biases in Deep-agent Emergent Communication
papers.research_question: Do sequence-processing neural networks exhibit natural language word-order biases, such as temporal iconicity, avoidance of redundancy, and minimization of long-distance dependencies?
papers.core_contribution: LSTM-based Seq2Seq agents show some natural language word-order biases (like avoiding long-distance dependencies) but not others (like avoiding redundant coding), suggesting the need to incorporate 'effort' to make AI communication more human-like.
papers.conclusion: Seq2Seq agents partially exhibit natural word-order biases, but differ in some aspects (like preference for backward order and weak redundancy avoidance), suggesting incorporating effort-based pressures to make AI communication more human-like.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM agents show a strong tendency to avoid long-distance dependencies.
LSTM agents have a preference for backward-iconic order over forward-iconic, which is opposite to human language.
Only weak tendency towards avoidance of redundant coding (e.g., markers in fixed-order languages).
In iterated learning, free-order languages tend to become more fixed with preferred orders emerging.
Attention-enhanced models learn faster and show some biases more clearly.
future_direction: How to incorporate 'effort'-based pressures in neural networks.
papers.abstract: Sequence-processing neural networks led to remarkable progress on many NLP tasks. As a consequence, there has been increasing interest in understanding to what extent they process language as humans do. We aim here to uncover which biases such models display with respect to "natural" word-order constraints. We train models to communicate about paths in a simple gridworld, using miniature languages that reflect or violate various natural language trends, such as the tendency to avoid redundancy or to minimize long-distance dependencies. We study how the controlled characteristics of our miniature languages affect individual learning and their stability across multiple network generations. The results draw a mixed picture. On the one hand, neural networks show a strong tendency to avoid long-distance dependencies. On the other hand, there is no clear preference for the efficient, non-redundant encoding of information that is widely attested in natural language. We thus suggest inoculating a notion of "effort" into neural networks, as a possible way to make their linguistic behavior more humanlike.

papers.title: Layer-wise Positional Bias in Short-Context Language Modeling
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether positional bias in language models is an intrinsic architectural property that persists across layers in short-context next-word prediction, independent of task complexity.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an attribution-based framework using layer conductance to analyze positional bias, showing that transformer layers exhibit stable, text-invariant positional importance profiles, with recency bias increasing with depth and early layers preferentially weighting content words.
papers.conclusion: LLM layers exhibit stable positional importance profiles in short-context next-word prediction, indicating positional bias is intrinsic to model architecture. Early layers assign the highest conductance to most words and prefer content words, while later layers lose word-type sensitivity and concentrate on recent positions.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer layers exhibit stable positional importance profiles in short-context next-word prediction.
These profiles are text-invariant and remain unchanged under lexical scrambling, indicating an intrinsic architectural property.
Recency bias increases monotonically with depth, while primacy bias is weak and diminishes in deeper layers.
Early layers preferentially weight content words over function words, while later layers lose this word-type differentiation.
Early layers dominate the largest proportion of words at all positions, while later layers increasingly concentrate importance on recent positions.
papers.limitation:
Focus on short contexts; may differ in long-context settings or tasks beyond next-word prediction.
Limited set of autoregressive transformer models; may not generalize to other architectures.
Reliance on layer conductance as a proxy for importance; different attribution methods may yield different results.
Word-type analyses based on POS categories and averaging; do not capture finer-grained syntactic or semantic distinctions.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to long-context regimes and tasks beyond next-word prediction.
papers.abstract: Language models often show a preference for using information from specific positions in the input regardless of semantic relevance. While positional bias has been studied in various contexts, from attention sinks to task performance degradation in long-context settings, prior work has not established how these biases evolve across individual layers and input positions, or how they vary independent of task complexity. We introduce an attribution-based framework to analyze positional effects in short-context language modeling. Using layer conductance with a sliding-window approach, we quantify how each layer distributes importance across input positions, yielding layer-wise positional importance profiles.
