The main finding is that such models rely primarily on collocational associations, followed by syntactic dependencies and coreference relationships, for next-word predictions.
papers.conclusion: The proposed token-wise decomposition provides an exact method to analyze model predictions without approximations, and analyses using it suggest collocational association and verbatim token repetition are key drivers of predictions in Transformer-based autoregressive language models.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed ∆LP importance measure shows weak correlation with layer-wise attention weights and gradient norms, indicating it captures a distinct quantity.
Regression analyses show Transformer-based language models rely most on collocational associations (PMI) for next-word predictions, followed by syntactic dependencies and coreference relationships.
Using ∆LP to predict syntactic dependencies shows performance varies by relation type, with higher precision for relations with strong collocational association (e.g., compounds, adjectival modifiers).
Using ∆LP for coreference antecedent selection shows high precision for proper and common nouns that are repeated verbatim, but low precision for pronouns.
The connection between model predictions and linguistic structures (syntax, coreference) appears to be largely driven by underlying collocational associations and token repetition.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is based on a model trained on English text and annotated English corpora, so findings may not generalize to other languages with different properties (e.g., more flexible word order).
The decomposition method is more computationally expensive to calculate than standard forward passes because it relies on an explicit decomposition of matrix multiplications, which are highly optimized in standard packages.
papers.abstract: While there is much recent interest in studying why Transformer-based large language models make predictions the way they do, the complex computations performed within each layer have made their behavior somewhat opaque. To mitigate this opacity, this work presents a linear decomposition of final hidden states from autoregressive language models based on each initial input token, which is exact for virtually all contemporary Transformer architectures. This decomposition allows the definition of probability distributions that ablate the contribution of specific input tokens, which can be used to analyze their influence on model probabilities over a sequence of upcoming words with only one forward pass from the model. Using the change in next-word probability as a measure of importance, this work first examines which context words make the biggest contribution to language model predictions. Regression experiments suggest that Transformer-based language models rely primarily on collocational associations, followed by linguistic factors such as syntactic dependencies and coreference relationships in making next-word predictions. Additionally, analyses using these measures to predict syntactic dependencies and coreferent mention spans show that collocational association and repetitions of the same token largely explain the language models' predictions on these tasks.

papers.title: Do Neural Language Models Show Preferences for Syntactic Formalisms?
papers.research_question: When probing language models for syntactic dependency structure, is Universal Dependencies (UD) the best fit, or is the representational structure better explained by Surface-Syntactic Universal Dependencies (SUD)? Are these patterns consistent across typologically different languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that neural language models (BERT and ELMo) encode syntactic structure that aligns better with the deep-syntactic style of Universal Dependencies (UD) than the surface-oriented Surface-Syntactic Universal Dependencies (SUD), and this preference is consistent across most languages and correlated with tree height differences.
papers.conclusion: The syntactic structure captured by neural language models aligns better with UD than SUD, and this alignment is influenced by linguistic factors and tree shape, with UD being a better fit for most languages.
papers.key_findings:
Both BERT and ELMo exhibit a preference for UD over SUD in most languages.
The preference for UD is stronger in languages with a high proportion of function words (like adpositions) and where SUD trees are significantly higher.
In agglutinative languages (Basque, Finnish, Turkish) the preference is less clear or even reversed.
The difference in tree height between UD and SUD is strongly correlated with the probing accuracy difference.
The probe performs best when combining information from multiple layers (weighted average).
papers.limitation: The probe combines two separate probes (distance and depth) and is not optimized for UAS directly, which may affect the validity of the extracted trees.
future_direction: Exploring probes that combine the distance and depth assumptions into a single transformation.
Methods for alleviating treebank supervision altogether.
Revisiting the insights within a non-probing framework, such as Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA).
papers.abstract: Recent work on the interpretability of deep neural language models has concluded that many properties of natural language syntax are encoded in their representational spaces. However, such studies often suffer from limited scope by focusing on a single language and a single linguistic formalism. In this study, we aim to investigate the extent to which the semblance of syntactic structure captured by language models adheres to a surface-syntactic or deep syntactic style of analysis, and whether the patterns are consistent across different languages. We apply a probe for extracting directed dependency trees to BERT and ELMo models trained on 13 different languages, probing for two different syntactic annotation styles: Universal Dependencies (UD), prioritizing deep syntactic relations, and Surface-Syntactic Universal Dependencies (SUD), focusing on surface structure. We find that both models exhibit a preference for UD over SUD -with interesting variations across languages and layers -and that the strength of this preference is correlated with differences in tree shape.

papers.title: The Grammar of Transformers: A Systematic Review of Interpretability Research on Syntactic Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: What do Transformer-based language models (TLMs) learn about syntax from the language modeling task?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a systematic review of 337 articles on syntactic knowledge in Transformer-based language models, identifying an over-focus on English and BERT, and finding that TLMs capture form-oriented syntactic phenomena well but perform more variably on phenomena at the syntax-semantics interface.
papers.conclusion: The review reveals a rich but heterogeneous landscape in syntactic interpretability research, with tentative evidence that formal syntax is easier for models than the syntax-semantics interface, and highlights the need for broader empirical scope and better data reporting.
papers.key_findings:
There is an over-focus on a single language (English) and a single model (BERT) in the literature.
TLMs perform better on formal syntactic phenomena (e.g., agreement) than on phenomena at the syntax-semantics interface (e.g., binding).
The field uses a balanced variety of interpretability methods (behavioral, mechanistic, probing), but probing has declined in recent years.
Multilingual and typological aspects of syntax are underexplored.
BLiMP benchmark scores show that model performance scales with training data size and that bidirectional models tend to outperform causal models for given data sizes.
future_direction: Reporting complete data in studies.
Better aligning theoretical constructs and methods across studies.
Increasing the use of mechanistic methods.
Broadening the empirical scope regarding languages and linguistic phenomena.
papers.abstract: We present a systematic review of 337 articles evaluating the syntactic abilities of Transformer-based language models, reporting on 1,015 model results from a range of syntactic phenomena and interpretability methods. Our analysis shows that the state of the art presents a healthy variety of methods and data, but an over-focus on a single language (English), a single model (BERT), and phenomena that are easy to get at (like part of speech and agreement). Results also suggest that TLMs capture these form-oriented phenomena well, but show more variable and weaker performance on phenomena at the syntax-semantics interface, like binding or filler-gap dependencies. We provide recommendations for future work, in particular reporting complete data, better aligning theoretical constructs and methods across studies, increasing the use of mechanistic methods, and broadening the empirical scope regarding languages and linguistic phenomena.

papers.title: When classifying grammatical role, BERT doesn't care about word order...\n except when it matters
papers.research_question: How do BERT and GPT-2 represent grammatical role (subject vs. object), and is this representation sensitive to word order, especially in sentences where lexical semantics are insufficient?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that while early layer embeddings in BERT and GPT-2 are dominated by lexical semantics, word order becomes crucial in later layers for representing grammatical role in non-prototypical sentences, allowing models to override lexical cues.
papers.conclusion: Considering non-prototypical instances is crucial for understanding how language models represent language, as the combinatorial power of syntax is most evident when expressing surprising or impossible meanings.
papers.key_findings:
Lexical semantics dominates early layer representations, while grammatical information is gradually acquired in later layers for non-prototypical sentences.
Models learn to represent the effect of syntactic word order on meaning independently from distributional information, as shown by accurate classification on argument-swapped sentences.
General positional information (e.g., primacy) is insufficient for grammatical role classification in non-prototypical cases; fine-grained syntactic word order is necessary.
Probing on average (prototypical) sentences obscures the gradual acquisition of syntactic information, which is only visible when analyzing non-prototypical cases.
The ability to understand non-prototypical meanings, a hallmark of human language, is present in the models' later-layer representations.
papers.abstract:
Because meaning can often be inferred from lexical semantics alone, word
order is often a redundant cue in natural language. For example, the words
chopped, chef, and onion are more likely used to convey "The chef chopped the
onion," not "The onion chopped the chef." Recent work has shown large language
models to be surprisingly word order invariant, but crucially has largely
considered natural prototypical inputs, where compositional meaning mostly
matches lexical expectations. To overcome this confound, we probe grammatical
role representation in English BERT and GPT-2, on instances where lexical
expectations are not sufficient, and word order knowledge is necessary for
correct classification. Such non-prototypical instances are naturally occurring
English sentences with inanimate subjects or animate objects, or sentences
where we systematically swap the arguments to make sentences like "The onion
chopped the chef". We find that, while early layer embeddings are largely
lexical, word order is in fact crucial in defining the later-layer
representations of words in semantically non-prototypical positions. Our
experiments isolate the effect of word order on the contextualization process,
and highlight how models use context in the uncommon, but critical, instances
where it matters.

papers.title: Garbage Attention in Large Language Models: BOS Sink Heads and Sink-aware Pruning
papers.research_question: What explains the layer-wise sensitivity and redundancy in LLMs, particularly in higher layers, and how can the <BOS> sink phenomenon be leveraged for effective pruning?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies <BOS> sink heads as a key mechanism for redundancy in LLMs and proposes a sink-aware pruning strategy that effectively removes redundant components with minimal performance loss.
papers.conclusion: The <BOS> sink phenomenon is a primary driver of functional redundancy in LLMs, and sink-aware pruning based on <BOS> sink scores provides an efficient and effective method for model compression, matching or exceeding established pruning methods.
papers.key_findings:
Heads with high <BOS> sink scores are functionally redundant, showing negligible impact on performance when ablated.
High <BOS> sink heads are concentrated in deeper layers, explaining the layer-wise sensitivity observed in pruning studies.
Pruning based on <BOS> sink scores outperforms magnitude- and activation-based methods (e.g., Wanda-SP, Mag-SP) in preserving downstream task accuracy.
The behavior of sink heads is stable across varying input sequence lengths, with higher-scoring heads showing more gradual decline in attention scores as sequence length increases.
The <BOS> sink score serves as a robust structural metric for identifying redundant heads and layers, enabling effective structured pruning.
papers.limitation:
The work is empirical and does not provide a formal theoretical derivation for the positional concentration of sink heads in deeper layers.
The study is limited to models of specific scales (e.g., 4B and 8B parameters) and may not generalize to ultra-large scale models.
future_direction: Validate the <BOS> sink phenomenon across larger-scale models and a broader range of downstream tasks.
Investigate whether similar attention-anchoring mechanisms exist in other Transformer-based architectures beyond text, such as Vision-Language Models (VLMs).
Study the developmental dynamics of sink heads during the pre-training phase to understand how they emerge.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to contain significant redundancy, yet a systematic explanation for why certain components, particularly in higher layers, are more redundant has remained elusive. In this work, we identify the BOS sink phenomenon as a key mechanism driving this layer-wise sensitivity. We show that attention heads with high BOS sink scores are strongly associated with functional redundancy: such heads, especially in deeper layers, contribute little to predictive performance and effectively serve as \emph{dumping grounds} for superfluous attention weights. This provides a concrete functional explanation for the structural redundancy reported in prior studies. Leveraging this insight, we introduce a simple pruning strategy that removes high-BOS sink heads. Experiments on Gemma-3, Llama-3.1, and Qwen3 demonstrate that this approach identifies redundant transformer components more reliably than weight- or activation-based criteria, while preserving performance close to dense baselines even under aggressive pruning. Moreover, we find that the behavior of sink heads remains stable across different sequence lengths. Overall, our results suggest that structural properties of attention offer a more intuitive and robust basis for model compression than magnitude-based methods.

papers.title: Language Models Are Greedy Reasoners: A Systematic Formal Analysis of Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: To what extent do large language models (LLMs) reason via chain-of-thought prompting, and do they rely on simple heuristics rather than genuine reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the PRONTO QA dataset and uses formal analysis to show that LLMs are capable of correct individual deduction steps but struggle with proof planning when multiple valid steps are available.
papers.conclusion: While the largest LLMs are generally capable of reasoning, they have difficulty with proof planning and selecting the correct proof step when multiple options are available.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are capable of making valid individual proof steps, even in fictional contexts.
LLMs have difficulty with proof planning: when multiple valid proof steps are available, they often select the wrong step, leading to incomplete proofs.
Real-world knowledge helps reasoning: performance is significantly better with true ontologies compared to fictional or false ones.
Longer proofs (5 hops) are challenging, especially with top-down traversal of the ontology.
For larger models, the main source of error is misleading steps rather than invalid steps.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to modus ponens, proof lengths of at most 5, and semantically simple sentences.
future_direction: Use PRONTO QA to compare LLM reasoning with human reasoning and explore which aspects of human reasoning LLMs acquired.
Develop reasoning systems with more sophisticated proof planning/search strategies, such as neurosymbolic approaches.
Investigate whether LLMs can produce longer proofs, reason with other deduction rules, or handle more semantically complex sentences.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable reasoning capabilities given chain-of-thought prompts (examples with intermediate reasoning steps). Existing benchmarks measure reasoning ability indirectly, by evaluating accuracy on downstream tasks such as mathematical reasoning. However, it is unclear how these models obtain the answers and whether they rely on simple heuristics rather than the generated chain-of-thought. To enable systematic exploration of the reasoning ability of LLMs, we present a new synthetic question-answering dataset called PrOntoQA, where each example is generated from a synthetic world model represented in first-order logic. This allows us to parse the generated chain-of-thought into symbolic proofs for formal analysis. Our analysis on InstructGPT and GPT-3 shows that LLMs are quite capable of making correct individual deduction steps, and so are generally capable of reasoning, even in fictional contexts. However, they have difficulty with proof planning: When multiple valid deduction steps are available, they are not able to systematically explore the different options.

papers.title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
papers.research_question: How can polysemantic interference structures in language models be exploited to manipulate model outputs, and do these interference patterns transfer across models of different scales and families?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that polysemantic interference structures in language models create a systematic vulnerability, and that interventions based on these structures, identified in small models, can transfer to larger instruction-tuned models for predictable behavioral control without requiring access to their internals.
papers.conclusion: Polysemantic interference reveals a systematic vulnerability in language models, and the generalization of these structures across scale and family challenges the view of polysemanticity as purely stochastic, offering new avenues for black-box control and theoretical insight into internal representation.
papers.key_findings:
Interventions leveraging polysemantic structures (feature-direction steering, token-gradient steering, prompt injection) can effectively manipulate model next-token predictions.
Polysemantic interference patterns are persistent across models: interventions distilled from small models (Pythia-70M, GPT-2-Small) transfer reliably to larger models (Llama-3.1, Gemma-2).
Many counterintuitive interference patterns are stable across models but remain largely opaque to human interpretation, suggesting models learn robust regularities not aligned with surface semantics.
Highly polysemantic neurons are more vulnerable to interventions; amplifying 'super-neurons' (activated by many features) strongly alters model behavior, while deactivating them has a reduced effect.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) whose outputs fluctuate with dimensionality and hyperparameters, yielding unstable features.
Interventions steer only one interference feature in one layer, while multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations could amplify and better obscure the effect.
Vulnerability is quantified solely via shifts in immediate next-token probabilities on two small base models, with only coarse transfer checks on larger instructed models.
future_direction: Establishing how these interventions alter non-trivial downstream tasks in bigger models.
Exploring multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations to amplify and better obscure intervention effects.
papers.abstract: Polysemanticity is pervasive in language models and remains a major challenge for interpretation and model behavioral control. Leveraging sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we map the polysemantic topology of two small models (Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small) to identify SAE feature pairs that are semantically unrelated yet exhibit interference within models. We intervene at four loci (prompt, token, feature, neuron) and measure induced shifts in the next-token prediction distribution, uncovering polysemantic structures that expose a systematic vulnerability in these models. Critically, interventions distilled from counterintuitive interference patterns shared by two small models transfer reliably to larger instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct), yielding predictable behavioral shifts without access to model internals. These findings challenge the view that polysemanticity is purely stochastic, demonstrating instead that interference structures generalize across scale and family. Such generalization suggests a convergent, higher-order organization of internal representations, which is only weakly aligned with intuition and structured by latent regularities, offering new possibilities for both black-box control and theoretical insight into human and artificial cognition.

papers.title: Internal Planning in Language Models: Characterizing Horizon and Branch Awareness
papers.research_question: To what extent are language models forward-looking and branch-aware in their planning, and how does the training objective (next-token vs. multi-token prediction) affect these qualities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an information-theoretic framework using VQ-VAE to analyze internal states of LMs, revealing task-dependent planning horizons, implicit preservation of alternative continuations, and concentration of decision-relevant information in recent layers and tokens.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework enables automated analysis of planning in LMs, revealing task-dependent planning horizons and branch awareness, and offers a scalable alternative to manual circuit discovery and probe-based methods.
papers.key_findings:
The effective planning horizon is task-dependent: longer horizons for tasks that require it, but myopic behavior for locally syntactic tasks.
Models implicitly preserve information about alternative correct continuations (branch awareness), with strength varying by task difficulty and model quality.
Next-token decisions draw most strongly on the last layers and the most recent token indices, though earlier blocks remain informative.
Training with multi-token prediction (MTP) loss modestly reduces purely myopic behavior compared to next-token prediction (NTP).
The proposed VQ-VAE-based pipeline provides a general-purpose, automated method for inspecting internal model dynamics without manual circuit engineering or probe-induced confounding.
papers.limitation:
The approach can only capture aggregate phenomena, providing insights in an average sense rather than interpreting individual input prompts.
The VQ-VAE compression necessarily discards some information, and the mutual information estimates are relative rather than absolute.
future_direction: Extend the framework to other model architectures.
Incorporate more fine-grained analyses.
Apply the framework to study other cognitive capabilities beyond planning.
papers.abstract: The extent to which decoder-only language models (LMs) engage in planning, that is, organizing intermediate computations to support coherent long-range generation, remains an important question, with implications for interpretability, reliability, and principled model design. Planning involves structuring computations over long horizons, and considering multiple possible continuations, but how far transformer-based LMs exhibit them without external scaffolds, e.g., chain-of-thought prompting, is unclear. We address these questions by analyzing the hidden states at the core of transformer computations, which capture intermediate results and act as carriers of information. Since these hidden representations are redundant and encumbered with fine-grained details, we develop a pipeline based on vector-quantized variational autoencoders that compresses them into compact summary codes. These codes enable measuring mutual information and analyzing the computational structure of the underlying model behavior. Using this framework, we study planning in LMs across synthetic grammar, path-finding tasks, and natural language datasets, focusing on two planning properties: (i) the planning horizon of pre-output computations, and (ii) the extent to which the model considers alternative valid continuations. As a separate downstream use of the same pipeline, we also analyze how decision-relevant information is distributed across layers and earlier prefix blocks when producing next-token predictions. Together, these analyses advance our understanding of planning in LMs and provide a general-purpose pipeline for inspecting internal model dynamics. Our results reveal that the effective planning horizon is task-dependent, that models implicitly preserve information about unused correct continuations, and that predictions draw most on recent computations, though earlier blocks remain informative.

papers.title: Language Modeling Teaches You More than Translation Does: Lessons Learned Through Auxiliary Syntactic Task Analysis
papers.research_question: How does the choice of pretraining objective (language modeling, translation, skip-thought, autoencoding) affect the learning of syntactic and part-of-speech information in LSTM models?
papers.core_contribution: Bidirectional language models learn more syntactic information than translation models, making them better for transfer learning on syntactic tasks, and untrained LSTMs retain input content better but trained models capture deeper syntactic features.
papers.conclusion: Bidirectional language models are more effective than translation models for learning syntactic information, and untrained LSTMs retain input content better but trained models capture deeper syntactic features.
papers.key_findings:
Bidirectional language models (BiLMs) outperform translation encoders on part-of-speech and CCG supertagging tasks.
BiLMs trained on 1 million sentences outperform other models trained on up to 63 million sentences.
Untrained LSTM baselines perform well on syntactic tasks when using ample classifier data, but performance drops more with less data compared to trained encoders.
Trained encoders underperform untrained ones on word identity prediction, indicating they capture genuine syntactic features beyond mere word memorization.
In LSTMs, the first layer is best for POS tagging, while the second layer can be better for CCG supertagging and predicting distant word identities, suggesting depth increases receptive field for abstract syntax.
papers.abstract: Recently, researchers have found that deep LSTMs trained on tasks like machine translation learn substantial syntactic and semantic information about their input sentences, including part-of-speech. These findings begin to shed light on why pretrained representations, like ELMo and CoVe, are so beneficial for neural language understanding models. We still, though, do not yet have a clear understanding of how the choice of pretraining objective affects the type of linguistic information that models learn. With this in mind, we compare four objectives—language modeling, translation, skip-thought, and autoencoding—on their ability to induce syntactic and part-of-speech information, holding constant the quantity and genre of the training data, as well as the LSTM architecture.

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: What Syntactic Structures block Dependencies in RNN Language Models?
papers.research_question: Do RNN language models learn specific syntactic island constraints that block filler-gap dependencies, or are they merely sensitive to gross syntactic complexity?
papers.core_contribution: RNN language models learn fine-grained syntactic constraints for filler-gap dependencies, specifically island effects, and can maintain other dependencies like gender expectations through islands, indicating differentiated learning of syntactic rules.
papers.conclusion: RNNs trained on language modeling learn both the unbounded nature and specific constraints of filler-gap dependencies, separating different dependencies with fine-grained syntactic rules.
papers.key_findings:
RNN models maintain filler-gap dependencies through unbounded sentential embeddings, showing sensitivity to hierarchical structure.
Models attenuate expectations for gaps in island constructions but not for gender expectations, indicating island constraints are specific to filler-gap dependencies.
Models learn left branch islands and show gradient sensitivity to coordination islands, but fail to learn sentential subject islands.
The Google model shows unbounded dependency maintenance, while the Gulordava model shows some degradation with depth, reflecting human-like performance limitations.
Model behavior on coordination islands is un-humanlike, with some residual expectations for gaps.
papers.limitation:
Models are conspicuously un-humanlike in some performance characteristics, such as on coordination islands.
Models fail to learn sentential subject islands.
papers.abstract: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) trained on a language modeling task have been shown to acquire a number of non-local grammatical dependencies with some success. Here, we provide new evidence that RNN language models are sensitive to hierarchical syntactic structure by investigating the filler--gap dependency and constraints on it, known as syntactic islands. Previous work is inconclusive about whether RNNs learn to attenuate their expectations for gaps in island constructions in particular or in any sufficiently complex syntactic environment. This paper gives new evidence for the former by providing control studies that have been lacking so far. We demonstrate that two state-of-the-art RNN models are are able to maintain the filler--gap dependency through unbounded sentential embeddings and are also sensitive to the hierarchical relationship between the filler and the gap. Next, we demonstrate that the models are able to maintain possessive pronoun gender expectations through island constructions---this control case rules out the possibility that island constructions block all information flow in these networks. We also evaluate three untested islands constraints: coordination islands, left branch islands, and sentential subject islands. Models are able to learn left branch islands and learn coordination islands gradiently, but fail to learn sentential subject islands. Through these controls and new tests, we provide evidence that model behavior is due to finer-grained expectations than gross syntactic complexity, but also that the models are conspicuously un-humanlike in some of their performance characteristics.

papers.title: Probing Syntax in Large Language Models: Successes and Remaining Challenges
papers.research_question: How do structural and statistical factors systematically affect the syntactic representations revealed by structural probes in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: This work analyzes the limitations and successes of structural probes for syntax in LLMs, finding they are sensitive to structural properties like linear distance and depth but not word predictability, and introduces a controlled benchmark for better evaluation.
papers.conclusion: Structural probes are more sensitive to structural properties (linear distance and depth) than statistical predictability, and while they have successes, they also have clear limitations that require further research.
papers.key_findings:
Structural probes are biased by linear distance: the closer two words are, the more likely they are predicted as syntactically linked.
Probes are challenged by deep syntactic structures and are misled by interfering nouns or ungrammatical verb forms.
Probe accuracy is not affected by the LLMs' predictability (surprisal) of individual words.
Despite challenges, probes reveal syntactic links more accurately than the raw activation space or a linear distance baseline.
Probes show some similarities to human parsing (e.g., attraction effects) but also clear failures, such as in simple prepositional phrase sentences.
papers.limitation:
Training data is strongly skewed toward dependencies with a linear distance of one, introducing bias.
If LLMs encode syntax along a nonlinear manifold, a strictly linear probe will distort that representation.
Some errors may originate from the LLMs themselves, which may fail to encode syntactic structure with full fidelity.
Prompting LLMs might affect their representations, and contextualizing sentences with a prompt could potentially enhance probe performance.
future_direction: Exploring non-Euclidean probes that better align with the geometry of LLM representations.
Training syntactic probes on controlled stimuli to better capture long-range dependencies and deeper hierarchical structures.
papers.abstract: The syntactic structures of sentences can be readily read-out from the activations of large language models (LLMs). However, the ``structural probes'' that have been developed to reveal this phenomenon are typically evaluated on an indiscriminate set of sentences. Consequently, it remains unclear whether structural and/or statistical factors systematically affect these syntactic representations. To address this issue, we conduct an in-depth analysis of structural probes on three controlled benchmarks. Our results are three-fold. First, structural probes are biased by a superficial property: the closer two words are in a sentence, the more likely structural probes will consider them as syntactically linked. Second, structural probes are challenged by linguistic properties: they poorly represent deep syntactic structures, and get interfered by interacting nouns or ungrammatical verb forms. Third, structural probes do not appear to be affected by the predictability of individual words. Overall, this work sheds light on the current challenges faced by structural probes. Providing a benchmark made of controlled stimuli to better evaluate their performance.

papers.title: Interpreting Emergent Planning in Model-Free Reinforcement Learning
papers.research_question: Can model-free reinforcement learning agents learn to perform decision-time planning internally?
papers.core_contribution: Provides the first mechanistic evidence that model-free RL agents can learn to plan internally, and introduces a concept-based interpretability procedure for investigating planning in such agents.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that model-free RL agents can learn to internally plan, and that the learned planning algorithm resembles bidirectional search, which is efficient for Sokoban.
papers.key_findings:
The DRC agent linearly represents planning-relevant concepts (Agent Approach Direction and Box Push Direction) in its ConvLSTM cell states, as shown by high probe accuracy.
The agent forms internal plans iteratively, using a process resembling parallelized bidirectional search, and refines plans with additional test-time compute.
Interventions on the agent's concept representations can steer its behavior, demonstrating that the plans causally influence action selection.
The planning capability emerges during training and coincides with the emergence of planning-like behavior such as benefiting from extra test-time compute.
Preliminary evidence suggests that similar planning mechanisms can be found in other architectures (ResNet) and environments (Mini PacMan).
papers.limitation:
The analysis is specific to Sokoban and a single agent architecture.
The methodology relies on having a good hypothesis for what concepts the agent might be using to plan.
The interventions are somewhat crude.
future_direction: Apply the methodology to other environments and agents.
Investigate whether similar planning mechanisms emerge in large language models trained with RL.
papers.abstract: We present the first mechanistic evidence that model-free reinforcement learning agents can learn to plan. This is achieved by applying a methodology based on concept-based interpretability to a model-free agent in Sokoban -- a commonly used benchmark for studying planning. Specifically, we demonstrate that DRC, a generic model-free agent introduced by Guez et al. (2019), uses learned concept representations to internally formulate plans that both predict the long-term effects of actions on the environment and influence action selection. Our methodology involves: (1) probing for planning-relevant concepts, (2) investigating plan formation within the agent's representations, and (3) verifying that discovered plans (in the agent's representations) have a causal effect on the agent's behavior through interventions. We also show that the emergence of these plans coincides with the emergence of a planning-like property: the ability to benefit from additional test-time compute. Finally, we perform a qualitative analysis of the planning algorithm learned by the agent and discover a strong resemblance to parallelized bidirectional search. Our findings advance understanding of the internal mechanisms underlying planning behavior in agents, which is important given the recent trend of emergent planning and reasoning capabilities in LLMs through RL

papers.title: Language Embeddings Sometimes Contain Typological Generalizations
papers.research_question: To what extent can neural network models learn generalizations about language structure, and how do we find out what they have learned? Which typological features can be discovered when the system is not told what to look for?
papers.core_contribution: This paper finds that neural models can sometimes learn typological generalizations in their language representations, but less readily than suggested by prior work, and that careful evaluation is essential to avoid false positives. It also releases several resources for 1295 languages.
papers.conclusion: Neural models can discover typological generalizations, but they do so less readily than suggested by previous research, and careful evaluation is necessary to confirm such discoveries.
papers.key_findings:
Some generalizations in learned language representations are surprisingly close to traditional typological features, but most models (including those from previous work) do not appear to have made linguistically meaningful generalizations.
Careful attention to evaluation details, such as controlling for genealogical and areal correlations, is essential to avoid false positives.
The word-level language model (WordLM) captures word order features and some morphological features, while many other models (including MTVec, MTCell, and Ö&T) show little evidence of encoding typological features when evaluated with their method.
Lexical baselines (ASJP and Lexical similarity vectors) do not encode structural features, as expected, and can serve as a baseline for evaluation.
papers.limitation: The study only tries to connect neural language representations with known features from the typological literature, not with potentially novel generalizations.
future_direction: Investigating whether models make typological generalizations that human linguists have not previously made.
papers.abstract: To what extent can neural network models learn generalizations about language structure, and how do we find out what they have learned? We explore these questions by training neural models for a range of natural language processing tasks on a massively multilingual dataset of Bible translations in 1295 languages. The learned language representations are then compared to existing typological databases as well as to a novel set of quantitative syntactic and morphological features obtained through annotation projection. We conclude that some generalizations are surprisingly close to traditional features from linguistic typology, but that most of our models, as well as those of previous work, do not appear to have made linguistically meaningful generalizations. Careful attention to details in the evaluation turns out to be essential to avoid false positives. Furthermore, to encourage continued work in this field, we release several resources covering most or all of the languages in our data: (i) multiple sets of language representations, (ii) multilingual word embeddings, (iii) projected and predicted syntactic and morphological features, (iv) software to provide linguistically sound evaluations of language representations.

papers.title: Transferring Linear Features Across Language Models With Model Stitching
papers.research_question: Can linear features (e.g., from Sparse Autoencoders, probes, and steering vectors) be transferred between language models of different sizes using affine mappings (model stitching), and what are the implications for efficiency and feature universality?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that affine mappings (stitches) between residual streams can effectively transfer linear features across language models, enabling compute-efficient training of Sparse Autoencoders and transfer of probes and steering vectors, while revealing differences in how semantic and structural features transfer.
papers.conclusion: Linear features can be transferred between language models via affine mappings, supporting weak universality and providing a method to improve the training efficiency of interpretability tools like Sparse Autoencoders.
papers.key_findings:
Using transferred SAEs as initialization can reduce FLOPs by ~50% when training SAEs on larger models.
Probes and steering vectors can be transferred between models with no additional training in specific cases (e.g., language steering).
Structural features (syntactic) transfer more consistently than semantic features, which are more polarized in transferability.
Specific functional features (e.g., entropy and attention deactivation features) preserve their roles after transfer.
Linear stitches support a weak universality hypothesis, showing that small and large models learn similar representation spaces.
papers.limitation:
Stitches are only trained on general internet text between models in the same family with the same tokenizer.
The scaling law analysis is theoretically incomplete due to lack of high-compute regime data to fit the irreducible loss.
The semantic/structural classification is imperfect and noisy due to reliance on another LLM for augmentations.
Probing and steering experiments are limited to particular tasks and settings.
future_direction: Verify findings in cross-family model settings and finetune stitches on special tokens or chat-templated data.
Explore other applications of stitches, such as transferring linear weight updates like LoRAs.
Expand probing and steering experiments to examine robustness and broader task settings.
papers.abstract: In this work, we demonstrate that affine mappings between residual streams of language models is a cheap way to effectively transfer represented features between models. We apply this technique to transfer the weights of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) between models of different sizes to compare their representations. We find that small and large models learn similar representation spaces, which motivates training expensive components like SAEs on a smaller model and transferring to a larger model at a FLOPs savings. In particular, using a small-to-large transferred SAE as initialization can lead to 50% cheaper training runs when training SAEs on larger models. Next, we show that transferred probes and steering vectors can effectively recover ground truth performance. Finally, we dive deeper into feature-level transferability, finding that semantic and structural features transfer noticeably differently while specific classes of functional features have their roles faithfully mapped. Overall, our findings illustrate similarities and differences in the linear representation spaces of small and large models and demonstrate a method for improving the training efficiency of SAEs.

papers.title: The Language Model Understood the Prompt was Ambiguous: Probing Syntactic Uncertainty Through Generation
papers.research_question: What is the extent of syntactic uncertainty in neural language models when processing temporary ambiguities, and how do disambiguating cues affect this uncertainty?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a generation-based method to probe syntactic uncertainty in language models, finding that LMs maintain multiple interpretations during temporary ambiguities and are sensitive to disambiguating cues, though with some errors.
papers.conclusion: LMs exhibit syntactic uncertainty by considering multiple analyses simultaneously, and while they are generally sensitive to disambiguating cues, they sometimes show errors indicating lingering misinterpretations or difficulty with agreement cues.
papers.key_findings:
LMs exhibit uncertainty over temporary syntactic ambiguities, tracking multiple analyses in parallel.
The degree of bias varies across ambiguity types (NP/S, NP/Z, Noun/Verb) and specific sentences.
Disambiguating cues often appropriately reduce uncertainty in favor of the correct analysis.
For NP/Z ambiguities, some completions show confusion about sentence structure, indicating lingering effects of initial misinterpretations.
For Noun/Verb ambiguities, LMs sometimes fail to use number agreement cues correctly.
papers.limitation:
Relying on automatic classification of sentences can introduce noise due to parser errors.
Cannot automatically detect ungrammatical completions or those with unclear analysis.
future_direction: Determine whether inter-item variation in LMs' preferences mirrors human expectations and/or corpus statistics.
Overcome limitations in automatic classification and detection of ungrammatical sentences.
papers.abstract: Temporary syntactic ambiguities arise when the beginning of a sentence is compatible with multiple syntactic analyses. We inspect to which extent neural language models (LMs) exhibit uncertainty over such analyses when processing temporarily ambiguous inputs, and how that uncertainty is modulated by disambiguating cues. We probe the LM's expectations by generating from it: we use stochastic decoding to derive a set of sentence completions, and estimate the probability that the LM assigns to each interpretation based on the distribution of parses across completions. Unlike scoring-based methods for targeted syntactic evaluation, this technique makes it possible to explore completions that are not hypothesized in advance by the researcher. We apply this method to study the behavior of two LMs (GPT2 and an LSTM) on three types of temporary ambiguity, using materials from human sentence processing experiments. We find that LMs can track multiple analyses simultaneously; the degree of uncertainty varies across constructions and contexts. As a response to disambiguating cues, the LMs often select the correct interpretation, but occasional errors point to potential areas of improvement.

papers.title: Why do LLaVA Vision-Language Models Reply to Images in English?
papers.research_question: Why do LLaVA-style vision-language models tend to reply in English when an image is included in the query, regardless of the query language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes Image-induced Fidelity Loss (IFL) in LLaVA models, finding the bias originates in the language backbone and can be mitigated by using bilingual language models or through a mechanistic intervention on intermediate attention layers.
papers.conclusion: Image-induced Fidelity Loss is a significant issue in LLaVA models, localized within the language model component. Improving the multilinguality of the underlying LLM is a promising path for building more robust multilingual VLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Adding an image to a query significantly reduces the probability of a LLaVA model replying in the same language as the query (Image-induced Fidelity Loss).
Replacing the monolingual language backbone (Vicuna) with a bilingual one (Yi or Leo) reduces IFL.
Visual inputs are mapped to a distinct region of the embedding space, separate from text embeddings of any language.
A simple mechanistic intervention (adding a language attribute vector to an intermediate layer) can substantially reduce IFL.
papers.limitation:
The debiased results rely on the assumption that the expert-annotated gold standard is correct, which may not be the case, especially for unfamiliar scripts.
The UMAP visualizations showing separation between image and text embeddings do not definitively prove they are mapped to distinct semantic spaces.
The study aggregates results across languages and does not focus on second- and third-order interactions or heterogeneous patterns of IFL between languages.
future_direction: Improving the mechanistic intervention through automatic attribute selection or better attribute construction.
Studying the broader class of fidelity loss in single-modality models.
Better understanding the heterogeneous patterns of IFL across languages.
papers.abstract: We uncover a surprising multilingual bias occurring in a popular class of multimodal vision-language models (VLMs). Including an image in the query to a LLaVA-style VLM significantly increases the likelihood of the model returning an English response, regardless of the language of the query. This paper investigates the causes of this loss with a two-pronged approach that combines extensive ablation of the design space with a mechanistic analysis of the models' internal representations of image and text inputs. Both approaches indicate that the issue stems in the language modelling component of the LLaVA model. Statistically, we find that switching the language backbone for a bilingual language model has the strongest effect on reducing this error. Mechanistically, we provide compelling evidence that visual inputs are not mapped to a similar space as text ones, and that intervening on intermediary attention layers can reduce this bias. Our findings provide important insights to researchers and engineers seeking to understand the crossover between multimodal and multilingual spaces, and contribute to the goal of developing capable and inclusive VLMs for non-English contexts.

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of Morphological Content in BERT Models for Multiple Languages
papers.research_question: To what extent do BERT-style models encode morphological feature information in their hidden representations and attention distributions for multiple languages?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that BERT-style models encode morphological information by partitioning their embedding space into convex regions correlated with feature values, that contextualized embeddings help disambiguate ambiguous forms but not completely, and that specific attention head/layer combinations focus on subject-verb agreement.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that pre-trained BERT-style models are sensitive to morphological information, with strong performance on feature-value classification and certain attention heads learning to focus attention in a manner consistent with morphological agreement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-style models partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value.
Contextualized embeddings allow models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases.
Specific attention head/layer combinations hone in on subject-verb agreement.
Supervision significantly aids in extracting morphological information, as unsupervised clustering performs near random baselines.
Morphological information is best represented in the middle layers for languages with complex morphology (German and Russian), while for simpler languages it is present throughout all layers.
papers.limitation:
Models have difficulty disambiguating syncretic (ambiguous) forms, especially in languages with complex inflectional morphology.
The classification tasks require supervision; unsupervised methods (k-means) perform near random baselines.
future_direction: Identifying morphological information in BERT-style models in an unsupervised fashion.
Improving models' ability to disambiguate syncretic forms for languages with complex inflectional morphology.
Further exploration of how morphological information is shared between words via self-attention.
papers.abstract: This work describes experiments which probe the hidden representations of several BERT-style models for morphological content. The goal is to examine the extent to which discrete linguistic structure, in the form of morphological features and feature values, presents itself in the vector representations and attention distributions of pre-trained language models for five European languages. The experiments contained herein show that (i) Transformer architectures largely partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value, (ii) the contextualized nature of transformer embeddings allows models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases, and (iii) very specific attention head/layer combinations appear to hone in on subject-verb agreement.

papers.title: Transformer Language Models without Positional Encodings Still Learn Positional Information
papers.research_question: Can transformer language models learn positional information without explicit positional encodings, and how do they do it?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer language models without explicit positional encodings (NoPos) can learn implicit positional information and achieve competitive performance, and this ability is due to the causal attention mask.
papers.conclusion: Transformer language models can learn positional information without explicit encodings, and this phenomenon is robust across settings but does not extend to masked language models, with the causal attention mechanism being the key factor.
papers.key_findings:
NoPos models achieve competitive perplexity compared to models with explicit positional encodings across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths.
Probing experiments show that NoPos models learn an implicit notion of absolute positions in their hidden representations, similar to models with learned positional embeddings.
The success of NoPos models is unique to causal language models; masked language models fail to converge without positional encodings.
Shuffling the prefix tokens leads to a dramatic increase in loss, indicating that the model uses the learned positional information.
The causal attention mask is conjectured to allow the model to infer absolute positions by counting the number of attendable tokens.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models up to 1.3B parameters, and while the trend suggests the findings should hold for larger models, this is not tested.
NoPos models are always slightly worse than models with positional encodings, indicating that the inductive bias of positional encoding is important.
papers.abstract: Causal transformer language models (LMs), such as GPT-3, typically require some form of positional encoding, such as positional embeddings. However, we show that LMs without any explicit positional encoding are still competitive with standard models and that this phenomenon is robust across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths.Probing experiments reveal that such models acquire an implicit notion of absolute positions throughout the network, effectively compensating for the missing information.We conjecture that causal attention enables the model to infer the number of predecessors that each token can attend to, thereby approximating its absolute position.Our findings indicate that causal LMs might derive positional awareness not only from the explicit positioning mechanism but also from the effects of the causal mask.

papers.title: CorrSteer: Generation-Time LLM Steering via Correlated Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we effectively steer large language models using Sparse Autoencoder features without requiring contrastive datasets or large activation storage?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CorrSteer, a fully automated pipeline that selects task-relevant Sparse Autoencoder features by correlating generation-time activations with task outcomes, and uses these features to steer model behavior with reduced side effects.
papers.conclusion: CorrSteer establishes correlation-based selection as an effective and scalable approach for automated SAE steering across diverse language model applications.
papers.key_findings:
CorrSteer improves performance on QA, bias mitigation, and safety benchmarks, e.g., +3.3% on MMLU and +27.2% on HarmBench.
Correlation-based feature selection is effective and scalable, requiring only inference-time activations and no contrastive data.
Multi-layer steering (CorrSteer-A, CorrSteer-P) outperforms single-feature steering, suggesting collaborative circuit effects.
CorrSteer reduces side effects compared to fine-tuning, as measured by the Side Effect Ratio (SER).
Selected features are semantically interpretable and align with task requirements (e.g., refusal features for safety, structured output for multiple-choice).
papers.limitation:
CorrSteer is static and cannot easily adapt to dynamic tasks or separate benign from harmful requests without additional context.
The method may capture spurious correlations rather than causal relationships, especially with limited samples.
future_direction: Extend CorrSteer to dynamic tasks and sequential decision-making.
Improve feature selection to further reduce spurious correlations.
Apply the method to larger models and more complex domains.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) can extract interpretable features from large language models (LLMs) without supervision. However, their effectiveness in downstream steering tasks is limited by the requirement for contrastive datasets or large activation storage. To address these limitations, we propose CorrSteer, which selects features by correlating sample correctness with SAE activations from generated tokens at inference time. This approach uses only inference-time activations to extract more relevant features, thereby reducing spurious correlations. It also obtains steering coefficients from average activations, automating the entire pipeline. Our method shows improved task performance on QA, bias mitigation, jailbreaking prevention, and reasoning benchmarks on Gemma-2 2B and LLaMA-3.1 8B, notably achieving a +3.3% improvement in MMLU performance with 4000 samples and a +27.2% improvement in HarmBench with only 108 samples. Selected features demonstrate semantically meaningful patterns aligned with each task's requirements, revealing the underlying capabilities that drive performance. Our work establishes correlation-based selection as an effective and scalable approach for automated SAE steering across language model applications.

papers.title: Analysis of argument structure constructions in a deep recurrent language model
papers.research_question: How does a recurrent neural language model process and represent different Argument Structure Constructions (ASCs)?
papers.core_contribution: The study demonstrates that a simple LSTM-based recurrent neural network can form distinct internal representations for different Argument Structure Constructions, with the strongest separation in the final hidden layer, supporting the hypothesis that hierarchical linguistic structure can emerge through prediction-based learning.
papers.conclusion: Even a relatively simple LSTM-based recurrent neural network can effectively differentiate between various Argument Structure Constructions, mirroring some aspects of human linguistic processing, and supporting its use as a computational tool in cognitive neuroscience.
papers.key_findings:
The LSTM model's sentence representations formed distinct clusters corresponding to the four ASCs (transitive, ditransitive, caused-motion, resultative) in all hidden layers.
The clustering was most pronounced in the final hidden layer, just before the output layer.
The model recognized the similarity between transitive and ditransitive sentences, keeping their clusters closer together.
The emergence of distinct ASC representations aligns with previous studies on word class and syntax rule representations in recurrent language models.
The findings suggest that recurrent neural networks can serve as effective computational analogs for studying linguistic processing in the human brain.
papers.limitation:
The custom dataset is limited to 2000 sentences and four specific ASCs.
The model used word IDs instead of embeddings, focusing on syntactic structures without semantic information.
LSTM networks diverge in critical ways from the neural mechanisms underlying language processing in the human brain and are not a biologically faithful account.
future_direction: Expand the dataset to include a wider variety of constructions and larger sentence pools.
Incorporate pre-trained word embeddings to study the interaction of semantic and syntactic information.
Validate the computational findings against empirical neuroimaging data (e.g., EEG, MEG) during continuous speech perception.
papers.abstract: Understanding how language and linguistic constructions are processed in the brain is a fundamental question in cognitive computational neuroscience. This study builds directly on our previous work analyzing Argument Structure Constructions (ASCs) in the BERT language model, extending the investigation to a simpler, brain-constrained architecture: a recurrent neural language model. Specifically, we explore the representation and processing of four ASCs-transitive, ditransitive, caused-motion, and resultative-in a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network. We trained the LSTM on a custom GPT-4-generated dataset of 2,000 syntactically balanced sentences. We then analyzed the internal hidden layer activations using Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) and t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) to visualize sentence representations. The Generalized Discrimination Value (GDV) was calculated to quantify cluster separation. Our results show distinct clusters for the four ASCs across all hidden layers, with the strongest separation observed in the final layer. These findings are consistent with our earlier study based on a large language model and demonstrate that even relatively simple RNNs can form abstract, construction-level representations. This supports the hypothesis that hierarchical linguistic structure can emerge through prediction-based learning. In future work, we plan to compare these model-derived representations with neuroimaging data from continuous speech perception, further bridging computational and biological perspectives on language processing.

papers.title: Large Language Models Are Partially Primed in Pronoun Interpretation
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) adapt their referential biases in pronoun interpretation in a human-like way when exposed to consistent referential patterns in the local discourse context?
papers.core_contribution: InstructGPT can adapt its syntactic bias in pronoun interpretation from exposure to referential patterns in the local context, but fails to adapt its semantic bias, suggesting LLMs only partially represent semantic knowledge in referential processing.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can adapt to syntactic patterns in pronoun interpretation from local exposure, but not to semantic patterns, indicating a partial and non-human-like representation of semantic knowledge in referential processing.
papers.key_findings:
InstructGPT adapted its syntactic bias (subject vs. non-subject preference) based on recent exposure, showing sensitivity to syntactic patterns in the local discourse.
InstructGPT exhibited a strong, persistent goal bias in pronoun interpretation that was not influenced by exposure to source/goal patterns, unlike human participants.
FLAN-UL2 failed to generate meaningful patterns, answering 'yes' 100% of the time to ambiguous target questions and showing poor comprehension.
The adaptation to syntactic patterns was observed even in the presence of confounding semantic goal bias (Experiment 2a).
The results suggest LLMs may over-represent semantic knowledge (goal bias) or lack the ability to track and adapt to higher-level semantic pattern frequencies across a discourse.
papers.limitation:
The study simulated participants only by manipulating the temperature hyperparameter; more sophisticated prompting methods could be explored.
Direct comparison with psycholinguistic experiments might not be the only method to investigate LLMs' discourse capacity.
The study is strictly behavioral and does not analyze the models' internal representations.
future_direction: Incorporate more detailed prompting to simulate diverse linguistic backgrounds in experimental simulations.
Mitigate the semantic knowledge gap via instruction fine-tuning or chain-of-thought prompting.
Explore a comprehensive list of discourse probing tasks as an alternative method.
papers.abstract: While a large body of literature suggests that large language models (LLMs) acquire rich linguistic representations, little is known about whether they adapt to linguistic biases in a human-like way. The present study probes this question by asking whether LLMs display human-like referential biases using stimuli and procedures from real psycholinguistic experiments. Recent psycholinguistic studies suggest that humans adapt their referential biases with recent exposure to referential patterns; closely replicating three relevant psycholinguistic experiments from Johnson & Arnold (2022) in an in-context learning (ICL) framework, we found that InstructGPT adapts its pronominal interpretations in response to the frequency of referential patterns in the local discourse, though in a limited fashion: adaptation was only observed relative to syntactic but not semantic biases. By contrast, FLAN-UL2 fails to generate meaningful patterns. Our results provide further evidence that contemporary LLMs discourse representations are sensitive to syntactic patterns in the local context but less so to semantic patterns. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/zkx06111/llm_priming.

papers.title: REFINER: Reasoning Feedback on Intermediate Representations
papers.research_question: How does interacting with fine-grained reasoning feedback on intermediate reasoning steps impact the performance of language models on reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REFINER, a framework where a generator LM iteratively refines its intermediate reasoning steps using structured feedback from a critic model, leading to improved performance on reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: REFINER demonstrates that structured, fine-grained feedback on intermediate reasoning errors significantly improves LM performance on reasoning tasks, and the critic model can serve as a reasoning refinement tool for LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
REFINER significantly outperforms baseline LMs of comparable scale on three diverse reasoning tasks (math word problems, synthetic natural language reasoning, and moral action generation).
The trained critic model alone can improve the reasoning of large LMs like GPT-3.5 without fine-tuning the reasoner.
Structured, fine-grained feedback is more beneficial for improving reasoning than scalar value feedback (e.g., from automatic metrics like BLEU).
Improving the generation of intermediate representations leads to better performance on the final answer prediction.
Training a generator with an imperfect (noisy) critic is still beneficial for performance.
papers.limitation:
The framework is not evaluated on all applicable downstream reasoning tasks due to their sheer number.
The critic model is task-specific, while an ideal critic would be general and capable of providing feedback on a wide range of reasoning tasks.
The considered fine-grained reasoning error types are specific to the chosen tasks and do not cover all possible error types.
future_direction: Generalizing the critic model to be capable of providing feedback on a wide range of reasoning tasks.
Generalizing the fine-grained reasoning error types beyond the tasks considered.
papers.abstract: Debjit Paul, Mete Ismayilzada, Maxime Peyrard, Beatriz Borges, Antoine Bosselut, Robert West, Boi Faltings. Proceedings of the 18th Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning is Subgraph Search: A New Lens on Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how fine-tuning works from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, viewing fine-tuning as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within the model's computational graph.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit-tuning, a fine-tuning method that dynamically localizes and optimizes subgraphs (circuits) within a model's computational graph, enabling analysis of learning dynamics and balancing task performance with general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Circuit-tuning provides a new method for studying learning dynamics from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, offering insights into how fine-tuning works and enabling more precise fine-tuning that balances task performance and general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit-tuning provides better training stability and preserves language modeling ability better than full fine-tuning.
The functionality of specific attention heads (Subject Attribute Heads) can reverse during fine-tuning to adapt to new tasks.
Some attention heads (Subject Identification Heads) preserve their functions and are shared before and after fine-tuning.
Nodes within a circuit cooperate through division of labor and indirect interactions to complete tasks.
Edges in the computational graph exhibit strengthening and weakening akin to Hebbian learning during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: The study of mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer a model to explain its behaviors. While recent studies have focused on the static mechanism of a certain behavior, the learning dynamics inside a model remain to be explored. In this work, we develop a fine-tuning method for analyzing the mechanism behind learning. Inspired by the concept of intrinsic dimension, we view a model as a computational graph with redundancy for a specific task, and treat the fine-tuning process as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within this graph. Based on this hypothesis, we propose circuit-tuning, an algorithm that iteratively builds the subgraph for a specific task and updates the relevant parameters in a heuristic way. We first validate our hypothesis through a carefully designed experiment and provide a detailed analysis of the learning dynamics during fine-tuning. Subsequently, we conduct experiments on more complex tasks, demonstrating that circuit-tuning could strike a balance between the performance on the target task and the general capabilities. Our work offers a new analytical method for the dynamics of fine-tuning, provides new findings on the mechanisms behind the training process, and inspires the design of superior algorithms for the training of neural networks.

papers.title: DREAMWALKER: Mental Planning for Continuous Vision-Language Navigation
papers.research_question: How can we enable strategic and interpretable planning for vision-language navigation in continuous environments?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DREAMWALKER, a world model based agent for VLN-CE that enables strategic planning through mental simulation in a discrete, structured abstraction of the continuous environment, leading to more interpretable and effective navigation.
papers.conclusion: DREAMWALKER demonstrates the effectiveness of world model based mental planning for strategic and interpretable vision-language navigation in continuous environments.
papers.key_findings:
DREAMWALKER outperforms prior model-free VLN-CE agents in terms of success rate and other navigation metrics.
Mental planning via MCTS in the internal world model is crucial for strategic navigation, outperforming greedy action selection.
The quality of the world model (specifically the scene synthesizer) directly impacts navigation performance, with perfect imagination providing an upper bound.
The accuracy of the distance estimation function is central to the planning process, with more accurate estimates leading to better performance.
The imagined future scenarios provide interpretability into the agent's decision-making process.
papers.limitation:
The scene synthesizer is trained on a limited dataset (61 scenes), restricting the quality and diversity of synthesized observations.
Mental planning may face computational challenges when scaling to larger, more complex environments, potentially slowing decision-making.
The agent is tested in static virtual environments; performance may be affected by dynamic elements (e.g., moving objects) in real-world settings.
There is a simulation-to-real gap, as the agent is developed and tested in a simulated platform.
future_direction: Improve the scene synthesizer, e.g., by using diffusion-based methods for higher quality synthesized views.
Develop strategies to handle dynamic changes in real-world environments.
Mitigate computational burden by maintaining a sliding buffer of navigation history.
papers.abstract: VLN-CE is a recently released embodied task, where AI agents need to navigate a freely traversable environment to reach a distant target location, given language instructions. It poses great challenges due to the huge space of possible strategies. Driven by the belief that the ability to anticipate the consequences of future actions is crucial for the emergence of intelligent and interpretable planning behavior, we propose DREAMWALKER -- a world model based VLN-CE agent. The world model is built to summarize the visual, topological, and dynamic properties of the complicated continuous environment into a discrete, structured, and compact representation. DREAMWALKER can simulate and evaluate possible plans entirely in such internal abstract world, before executing costly actions. As opposed to existing model-free VLN-CE agents simply making greedy decisions in the real world, which easily results in shortsighted behaviors, DREAMWALKER is able to make strategic planning through large amounts of ``mental experiments.'' Moreover, the imagined future scenarios reflect our agent's intention, making its decision-making process more transparent. Extensive experiments and ablation studies on VLN-CE dataset confirm the effectiveness of the proposed approach and outline fruitful directions for future work.

papers.title: Order-sensitive Shapley Values for Evaluating Conceptual Soundness of NLP Models
papers.research_question: How well do deep NLP models learn word order, and are they conceptually sound with respect to order-sensitive linguistic concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Order-sensitive Shapley Values (OSV), a model-agnostic explanation method for attributing importance to word order in sequential data, and uses it to show that many NLP models are not conceptually sound with respect to word order.
papers.conclusion: Order-sensitive Shapley Values (OSV) provide a faithful explanation method for evaluating conceptual soundness of NLP models, revealing that models often ignore word order and are not conceptually sound.
papers.key_findings:
